There are no branch community offices outside the SE of England which seems absurd and London-centric. It's disappointing as it feels like Lloyds are one of few major employers to place major focus elsewhere in the country, but then don't consider the plethora of issues people outside London face, like diabolical public transport.

My advice would be to establish a culture of 'anchor days' - of no specific frequency but team lead driven for when it feels necessary. In-person anchor days could be earmarked for collaboration, learning and team bonding - and then otherwise leave office attendance to the discretion of the employee? The employees not attending on anchor days would much more visible and detrimental to the business than someone who doesn't attend an arbitrary 40% of time but is present for all in person and online collaboration.

Arbitrary 40% in office rule that feels against the Lloyds value of Trust. I'm very happy to, and do come into office to collaborate if my teammates are there and collaboration is earmarked for that day. But otherwise to sit at a desk on my own in a noisy environment, still take meetings on Teams and pay lots!!!! of money on extortionate and unreliable trains and adding 3/4+ hours of redundant travel to my day feels pointless, frustrating for me and my family who rely on me, and against all logic. 

Very difficult for employees who live in regional towns or rural areas.

Driving people towards large cities through enforcing presence like this only exacerbates issues like cost of living/homelessness.

If the majority of large employers were to allow greater employee choice of working location with no detriment to the business (see advice), this could have more of an impact socially and environmentally than lots of the work that occurs within Lloyds to combat these issues.

summary: Focus on "Going Faster" is resulting in demoralised employees
advice:
Main thing is to stop pushing people to be faster and start to listen to what staff are feeling? Change is necessary, but the way you are goin about this is simply not conducive to a good workplace. You will lose (and indeed have) very experienced and good members of staff.

When you carry out staff surveys, nothing ever seems to come from it, and focussing on just the positive aspects (which isn't many) is simply not the right way to treat staff who do have opinions and in many cases a much clearer and better view of what goes on at the frontline.
pros:
Some of the best reason for working at Lloyds are:
1. Salary package and benefits
2. Pension
3. Team members
cons:
Over the past year the Bank has decided that in order to compete with smaller Fintechs, they need to increase speed to market of digital technology and services. Now this in principle is a good idea, but in reality it is poorly executed. 

Communication of the new ways of working (LBG's favourite buzzword) is simply attrocious and many (if not most) people simply do not understand the direction we are heading. 

Implementation of new technology and systems to make things agile is adding additional complexity and processes to get things done. Internal communication has become a minefield and with structure changing almost on a monthly basis, many people are fed up and tired of Senior Leadership spouting the same things over and over again.

Another new restructure and way of working is due at the tail end of the year and again people are asking question of Senior Leaders and being told all is good, when on the front line, it is clearly not. 

People are being told to accept that change is necessary and effectively ignoring the majoroty of staff when they tell them thinsg are not working. 

Overall it does not feel a good place to work right now. The main changes in this organisation has came ever since the current CEO Charlie Nunn took over from Antonio and effectively removed most of the Senior Leaders and replaced with people who knew Charlie from the past. Many of these people clearly do not understand or conform to the LBG culture that many of us have worked for years and see a rapid decline in good feeling within the organisation.

summary: The good and the bad (mainly the latter)
advice:
Be more transparent; don't forget the customer; treat colleagues as the key resource they are; Listen (rather than pretend to); reassess band F and G resourcing as there is a layer in 
junior/ lower middle-ish management that isn't providing value for money; continue to focus on data and technology upgrades; a laser focus on profitability is absolutely fine, but if you want that to be sustainable you need to make sure customers and colleagues are happy and engaged.
pros:
Competitive benefits package (although being eroded)
Broadly a 35hr week
Some flexibility (two days in the office three from home)
Senior leadership trying to resolve legacy issues, old systems and data issues to make up for decades of neglect.
Large company so (in theory) you can move around, learn new skills and develop and progress your career.
Still an okay company compared to others, although two or three years ago, this was a very good company compared to others. And other companies aren't raising their game, we are lowering ours. Up until recently LBG was the best company I had worked for (and I've worked for a number of our competitors), but now there is no real differentiator, and in some cases we are lagging behind.
cons:
Benefits being eroded by the senior leadership team
Flexible working eroded and changes poorly communicated which has seriously damaged trust and morale.
A focus on profit and growth but not necessarily on customer and seeing lots of decisions being made that will likely be tomorrow's scandal.
Slow, painful, decision making, and committees for everything.
Complex business and silos
Dependency on contractors who year after year fail to bed in sustainable, permanent, repeatable processes....and why would they 😁
Offices are generally horrible, dirty and depressing places (although this is being looked at)
Record profits yet lower bonuses - not sure how that works.
Massive change in culture since the new CEO came in - some positives in terms of driving the business forward, but offset by terrible communication, a focus on profit and sales (to the detriment of customers based on what I've been involved in).
A lot of people simply not qualified to do the job they are in. People with no investment experience in investment teams, people in risk teams with no risk experience and/or business experience. 
Culture below Board level of massaging or hiding bad news.
Tick box Risk and Compliance, and likely to get worse following "rationalisation".
Recruitment is a shambles - if you want to give GIA some work, they could look at this process, the lack of transparency, and the candidate selection decisions taken.

summary: My Experience at Lloyds Banking Group
pros:
-The pay for the level of experience needed was great - at the time it was around £21,000 a year before tax.
-Work environment was supportive and friendly, everyone got along and there was no real drama in my area.
-Continental Shifts (4 days of 11 hour shifts, then 4 days off)
-Felt supported regarding internal progression goals
cons:
-No time between phone calls, you are WORKING for those 11 hours (minus 1 hour lunch break) and you have to be switched on the whole time. Dealing with other people's money and bank accounts, mistakes are a big deal.
-Very monotonous work - sat at a desk, staring at a screen, from sunrise to sunset.
-Harsh reviews with managers. A lot of calls take longer - it's mostly people with very difficult questions, or old people who are very confused and don't understand anything no matter how many times you explain things to them. The longer call times are seen negatively by managers.
-Burnout is very real,
-Less benefits each year (they used to offer base rate mortgages to their employees, but stopped the year I started working there!)

You will essentially become just another number, spending hours answering back-to-back calls from angry, rude, and disrespectful customers. Your times on each call and the 10 second break you get to write your notes is constantly monitored. 
Worse, you will receive little to no support from management. If you're stuck on a difficult call and need a manager’s assistance, be prepared to wait a long time. Managers don’t have to deal with the calls anymore, so they treat it as "your problem."

The workplace culture focuses solely on negative feedback, with little to no recognition for the positive things you accomplish. Even if you follow the correct procedures, if something goes wrong, the blame falls on you.

Additionally, the responsibilities seem to keep growing after you start, with many tasks not included in the original job description. When you raise concerns, the response is simply, "We all have to deal with it."

If you're thinking of leaving your current job for this one, don't.

advice:
Hire more (direct permanent) employees, less outsourcing and partner companies. Approach more technically brilliant people and hire them. Form a few small core teams (like startups) with strict high standards only comprised of permanents. Ones that you could trust in terms of delivering & good decisions, then give them more freedom, more responsibility and grow them.  A few "islands of technical culture" nuclear trustable core teams, that they can hire too. Keep track of and review the long-term performance of the software of those people -- who left for different teams.  Provide visa sponsorship to access brilliant employees. There is already a vetting process. To avoid unknown untraceable background of international (for vetting) just make it necessary to have worled/lived a few years in the country (ask for UK work experience).  It will be necessary to find people who can choose good people, but those need to be from the new hires.
I can provide more details about this particular plan and the way that I call "incubated autonomous nuclei of excellence".
In general, upgrade the legacy to newer versions, even if at a high cost. On the other hand, the issue of trust of managers to the technical ability of engineers. This is the root of the use of partner companies. Hire more brilliant people and let them work together to form nuclei of brilliance. Leave room for creativity, by pursuing multiple streams of something, and then choose the best approach. You will end up spending much less money on things in the long term.
pros:
Recommended if you want to get experience in large professional teams with advanced processes. What you will engineer, will be used in real life, will have a large impact, and what you do will be used potentially by millions of people. Many teams, Good Agile, Disciplined, Good & skilled scrum master, automated tests, CI/CD. Good management: supportive, and respectful (if they are from LBG itself, not partner companies). 
Exposure to large corporate management style and organisation. 
Technically, If you are interested in Banking or Security, or both, it can be great. Opportunities are given for you to grow (managerial). Encourage you to take courses in cloud technology. Multi-Cloud exposure. DevOps skills are valued a lot. Highly paced, delivery. Paid well, continuous salary increase. Computer Security, Web, Cloud. You feel supported by diversity, job security, benefits, & health support. Respectful behaviour by LBG employees. Compensations and benefits are good. From time to time you will find out that your salary has increased for random reasons. Actively initiation to improve test coverage, test automation, BDD, etc. If you like software management, if you want to become an architect. If you want to learn agile or become scrum master, etc, it is recommended. Willing to bring new technologies, such as the newest cloud platforms. Things change, and technologies will arrive. You see less or no ego (at least on the surface). Management is ready to solve any issues and support you at various levels (including health). In a way, management is self-aware and honest, but politically correct. Since the pandemic, it stayed fully remote. I realised maternity benefits were great. During the 2-3 years, there was a lot of advancement in technical abilities and learned lessons. A true transformation (but naturally slowed down by the vast size of the organisation and the complexity of decision processes with multiple people ).
cons:
The official process of things can be complex and you may have a limited scope. Of course, high-security sensitivity may slow things down (but you are paid for that). Of course legacy code. Sometimes it feels like it is vast, like a country, which is interesting (especially from the point of view of management and organisation), but you have visibility about a small part. There is a legacy of outsourcing mindset in the past. But there is awareness about them. The new decisions are better and I felt the transformation in various aspects. 
Sometimes legacy & brand lock-in, but you are paid high for such inefficiencies that are typical of large corporates.

Lack of Meeting Space: The limited availability of meeting rooms and collaborative spaces exacerbates the situation. This leads to a noisy working environment due to constant calls and meetings, negatively impacting productivity. advice:
Woled for Lloyds for over 12 years and left due to mental health reasons. I had finally had enough of the toxic culture and environment that is Lloyds Bank. There is a consistent high turnaround of staff, especially within the customer service departments which should be an instant red flag to anyone thinking of applying to work with Lloyds. Managers there are typically ones who have been in the job for decades and have no desire to progress and are just awaiting their retirement or people who have been pre selected before interviews have even begun because their 'face fits'. About 70% of the Managers within customer service (especially fraud) are absolutely useless. No common sense and couldn't lead a horse to water if they tried never mind a team of 14/15 people. Etc etc. Before I left, management sent out an email requesting people who were reporting an absence due to illness, to call in via teams video chat. Who wants to do that when you're ill? Needless to say, this was reported to the Union, but its things like this that management will try and get away with. 
I moved away from customer service to Business Management and Needless to say the grass wasn't greener. Left after a few months and there was nothing in way of a leavers interview, no call from anyone in management to thank me for over 12 years service, not even a goodbye card. Nothing. They pretend to care, but they don't. You are and always will be, just a number to them.

summary: "People First" - Unless you're a senior manager
advice: If you really believe only a minority of people feel this way, do an anonymous vote of confidence in your leadership abilities. If you lose, leave. If you're aware of how bad it actually is, please start living the company values you've set and do something about it.
pros:
Benefits package is generous including 30 days annual leave and 15% pension contribution. The people are great.
Every day flexibility, if you need to run an errand during the day, you have the freedom to do that around meetings.
cons:
One of the companies values is "People-First - we put people first to go further for customers. We listen and care for people as individuals. We go the extra mile to help customers, colleagues and communities feel more supported, in control and confident about their future"

This is how the senior leaders have lived this value over the last year:

1. Announced a mandated return to office, for 40% of your time, without providing any evidence for the benefits they claimed. This includes people who were hired remotely, the other side of the country from the team they work with, who now have to travel into their local office, with no one they know, because of "collaboration".
2. At the same time, announced removing consolidated working arrangements that had been in place to support those caring for sick family members, newborn babies, etc. They replaced this with a policy putting a limit on the length of these agreements. There are now people having to ration their holiday allowance to use to take time off to care for family members.
3. In response to the above two announcements, thousands of people spoke out against it in the comments on the article, but employee's concerns were brushed off as people "struggling with change".
4. A follow-up announcement included all senior leaders piling into the comments section voicing their support for the changes, while replying in very passive aggressive ways to people who didn't, asking those people to have a "chat to understand why they feel this way". This led to people not feeling comfortable sharing their opinion.
5. Subsequent announcements had comments turned off, preventing people voicing their opinion.
6. A survey was released promising to 'listen to colleagues' on this subject, which included loaded questions forcing you to pick between 'I care about the company' and 'I don't see the value in the changes'.
7. Contract changes, removing any right to redundancy packages if you reject a role they arbitrarily think you're suitable for, even if it's nothing to do with your skillset and requires a complete change in your career aspirations.
8. Changes to restrict internal applications. Managers are notified automatically if you apply for another role and you can only apply to one role at a time. This will heavily dissuade some colleagues from applying and enables managers to prevent you moving roles if it's not in their interest.
9. Pay increases have been significantly below inflation. This is constantly eroding employees buying-power, during a cost of living crisis, while selling it as a positive thing we should be grateful for and the bank also announcing a 57% increase to pre-tax profits.
10. Locking in a two year pay deal, passing the risk of a significantly volatile economic environment onto employees.
11. Disingenuously using PR and spin that a political would be proud of on all internal announcements. Including one off payments into year on year salary comparisons. Using forecasts from the BOE in their announcements to staff around pay to make the offer look competitive, but then just a few days later releasing their own forecasts via a company report that were higher. 
12. Re-worked some offices to be open plan unproductive hell-holes. Conveniently, senior leaders have their own private and quiet offices, where they don't have to deal with the sensory insanity around them while still trying to focus on work.

Due to all of the above employee morale is at an all time low. Charlie Nunn in a recent all-colleagues call brushed this off as a 'minority' of people feeling that way, but I haven't met a single colleague who isn't feeling deflated and under appreciated because of everything that's happened. 

In a single year the senior leadership team has destroyed the morale, trust and goodwill of a workforce that's taken years to build.

advice: Listen to your colleagues and fix the things that matter
pros: Pension scheme and contribution rates Ability to buy holidays Benefits providers The majority of staff are brilliant people
cons: Lloyds Banking Group used to be a great place to work however recent changes to its leadership team are rapidly eroding the trust, goodwill and enjoyment of colleagues within the Group. This current incumbent leadership confuse pace for progress with several recent people-led decisions brutally enforced to the detriment of thousands of colleagues. There is an air of distrust about the leadership evidenced by an unwillingness to listen to colleague voice, but also in their determination to plough their will at any cost. Instead of engaging with, and capturing the hearts and minds of colleagues, this leadership team seems hell bent on destroying the fabric of this once great organisation. Archaic and frankly backwards changes to things like 'flexible working arrangements' and it's assault on stamping out compressed working patterns, so often the great leveller for female and geographical fairness, is now reflective of the decision making being executed at the top level. Pair this if you will, with the irony that the organisation will also produce reports on topics such as the gender pension gap but fail to acknowledge its own role in being a leading contributor to this issue. The new leadership team have instilled a culture of fear, where the ability to speak up and out across key things once considered important to the business, is now met with a view that if you don't tow the party line then here is the door. This can be further supported by the most recent of colleague surveys once aimed at measuring engagement which now seek to place people in the camp of being either in love with the organisation or not, and this extremely polarity of responses enables the Group to marginalise those whom don't answer the correct response. Instead of using data driven decisions, major changes are now made for it's people strategy that feel more driven by viewpoints and niggles - rather than by what actually matters. Another side to the Group is that it's relentless focus on excelling rapid promotions of those from university educated backgrounds has created a raft of leaders whom are incapable of challenging upwards, and whom lack real leadership behaviours. This not only creates a new element of bias and a lack of diversity of thought but also often ignores the experience and ability of longer serving colleagues whom often end up overlooked for promotions. A great example is that the business is now more obsessed with 'what people say' as appose to what their output is, with initiatives in my last area often being immeasurably vague or just frankly tackling the wrong problem. Once again - pace vs progress. My final observation is that this is now a business with some of the most confusing communicators I have ever come across in my time there. There are now very senior figures whom struggle to articulate and answer questions or challenges on divisional calls and do not seem to be able to outline a clear strategy. This often leads to a complete lack of confidence and trust in those leaders and colleagues becoming disillusioned with the Groups actual vision. An example of this is with senior leaders using outlandish headlines to justify changes like 'we need to change now, to be here in 5 years time'. Let's not forget, LBG is the biggest UK bank, I'm fairly confident it will never fail... financial results and publicly available reports show you that's in pretty good shape. This current narrative from senior leaders ignores honesty and integrity and instead uses it as a shield to hide behind. It saddens me that this once great organisation is now creating a really difficult place for many colleagues to work. Some people might see this review as someone who's just had a bad experience but I'd point you to the data that's readily available on here to see. A quick look at the review graph for this Group shows an organisation that at the end of last year scored over 4, and yet just 10 months later finds itself at 3.3 and falling, ask yourself - can't just be me right?

advice: Get real or go home. You've ripped the heart out of work teams and from what I'm hearing (when I struggle into the office) you've also caused immense upheaval for hard working families too. pros: Struggling to think of any
cons: Was recruited into this role less than 2 years ago when we were just coming out of lockdown and hoping to return to some normality. I'm a cloud services specialist and although I wasn't head-hunted as such I did get a "tap on the shoulder" from a mate who works at Lloyds, knew my skill set and told me there were opportunities coming up as Lloyds looks to move much of it's architecture to Cloud over the next few years. Having always worked for smaller companies I had my reservations and told my pal I didn't think the huge corporate environment was for me. And I wouldn't fit in. He put my fears to bed by explaining that the bank had a strong people culture and that right at the heart of it was flexible working including WFH and varied working patterns. So based on this recommendation and a decent interview and salary offer I made the move. The first 12 months were great. The team made me feel very welcome and I hit the floor running. Let's just say my experience was significantly ahead of many of my new teams mates but I was happy to share knowledge and help them improve. I get on great with my immediate boss and there was talk of promotion within 12 months of me arriving. Then BOOM out of the blue the rug has been pulled. Get in the office 2 days a week says Charlie Nunn. I've been an IT professional for over a decade and a half and never been dictated to like this. My nearest office is an hour away and the office where my actual colleagues are based is even further. But that's not the half of it. I took the job based on an agreement with the hiring manager that I'd have Monday off and work my hours over 4 days. I do this for very personal reasons but I give back so many hours by working late or at weekends to solve problems in my own time. Sounds sad I know but when I have a problem in my head I can't rest until I've solved it. So now I'm regretting coming to this place. Not because of my immediate boss or the team. Or even the work or the workload. It's because some dictator in his wood panelled office has decided that grown adults can't be trusted to work from home and can't get through their workload in 4 longer days. Well get this Mr Nunn and the board. You are so out of touch with the real world. You can try to convince us that we need to adhere to your mantra because we're doing a huge transformation etc etc. But you'll have to do it without me I'm afraid. I'll be out of here by the end of this year and back working somewhere that's more progressive and forward thinking. I'd like to say thanks for my time here but I'll save that for my team mates at my leaving doo. Good luck hiring and retaining the IT specialists you're going to need to make your "huge transformation" into reality.

summary: Backtracking On What Makes Us Great
advice: Start listening to your staff again.
pros: A wide range of roles and locations, given it is such a large company. Encouragement to develop colleagues and many options for progressing your career within. A positive track record on Inclusion and Diversity.
cons: Current senior management have lost their way. The group has been making a lot of progress in the last 5+ years with reducing geographical and other institutional barriers to career progression (lifting requirements for all teams to be based out of a single office, embracing technology that allows us to more effectively collaborate across distances, giving local management the ability to work with their teams to flex schedules to accommodate both improved work/life balance and the needs of the team, etc). Unfortunately in April 2023 company-wide one-size-fits-all policies regarding in-office time and the removal of long-term compressed/alternative working patterns. Non-fixed office staff are now being required to spend 40%+ of their hours in physical office locations set up in call centre like open plan hubs (many with both desk and parking capacity issues due to other office closures in the last 5 years), regardless of where their teammates are located, and their own needs to complete their work effectively. Rigidity in the new policies makes no allowances for existing (including pre-pandemic) team/colleague arrangements, and only provide limited accommodation where required by law (eg Disabilities Act). Local management were blindsided with these changes, and are between a rock and a hard place trying to support their staff to comply, using insufficient FAQs and sources of support. Many FAQ responses amount to “we don’t care how much upheaval and cost this will generate for you, or if you think it will have a negative impact on your work. We think we know what will benefit 60k people better than their local management, and you’re just being obstructionist if you don’t agree”. A 5 star organisation has become a 3 star nearly overnight.

summary: Think very carefully before applying or joining
advice: It feels the second coming of Liz Truss and Brittania Unchained - a leadership that lives a completely different life to its staff declaring war on their laziness telling them the pandemic and all the adjustments people made were a benefit the company gifted to them that they should be grateful for. Leaders need to leave your ivory tower for a week, try daily sorting your own child / elder care on a low salary, try finding your own desk every morning, try concentrating whilst there are noisy conversations all around you, try juggling inflexible school hours with reality of public transport outside London. Don't do it for your employees, this is the reality of life your customers have to lead, it would do you good to feel and experience it instead of just reading a spreadsheet about it.
pros: Private medical, training Bear in mind though arbitrarily the company launches "new deals" which is a byword for removal of benefits you thought you had when you joined. It enjoys a cosy relationship with an in house union that nods through everything so the company can side-step statutory consultation. Whatever they tell you in the advert or on joining, you can expect to have changed if not before you start, certainly within 12 months and not for the better. Company ideally wants candidates of graduate quality (but not at graduate pay rates) in their 20s unencumbered with caring responsibilities and baggage who'll put in long hours to grab experience and then shove off elsewhere before they acquire life responsibilities like kids, elder care, disabilities and then start to become a burden and a nuisance. It's a blue-chip consulting firm transactional model but with pound-shop cheapness. If that's what you need at this point in your career then go for it. Lloyds will certainly give you more experience than your grade would normally command because it's chronically short-staffed so there are endless opportunities to step up and do things as long as you don't expect to be paid for the responsibility. Then after 18 months clear off somewhere else. Don't give / expect any loyalty or longevity and you'll be fine. Some people do well on pay advancement by flipping in and out of Lloyds - external experienced hires are nearly always paid more than internal promotions.
cons: This is all in public domain. "New deals" is the phrase for reduction of benefits. This includes - "new deal" repackaging of the bonus to disguise well below inflation pay rises. "New deal" dividing staff into different pay markets to disguise giving some people intra year pay rises for some jobs not others. "New deal" halving redundancy pay. "New deal" transferring jobs to India. "New deal" forcing people to work in an office (doesn't matter where or whether your team are located there) 2 days a week with Orwellian surveillance to police and ensure the company knows "where you are", in the name of productivity. "New deal" buildings with insufficien desks so you get told which days you're allowed in and may get a stool and a touch down desk to work at all day. "New deal" on flexible working, apprently the company is too flexible so new deal is you either work full-time or part-time in whole days like the 1990s. Apparently staff had too good a time during the pandemic. New deal sees disabled staff and those with caring responsibilities pleading their cases on internet forums and with management to justify exemptions, it's degrading. New deal is temporary flexibility for moments that matter - Caring for elders is regarded as a temporary "moment that matters" where you've 3 months to devise a care plan either to build a nursing home to resolve the lack of care spaces in your area, win the lottery to pay for it, give up work to become a carer or tell your relative to have a Lazarus moment and get themselves well. New deal: work late nights or the weekend and looking for some time back to recover - well tough because everyone has to work a minimum seven hour day regardless. What's not changed is leadership retain quiet private offices and an entourage of staff to support them.

summary: Excellent work life-balance. Great place to work.
advice: Continue to modernise the banks technology; websites and apps. Make sure all tech is done in-house to cut costs and make sure talent and skills are kept in house. Were possible close offices and branches to remove the financial burden and prepare the bank for the digital age. The remaining branches should be located in cities only and provide a free co-working space and drinks and cakes for customers for a small fee. Almost like a perk for banking with LBG. Allow colleagues to work remotely from home and abroad for 1 month a year. Expand the list of countries that can be worked from abroad, make it an official reward and ensure the application process is via HR and not line managers. Ensure that all colleagues that are meeting the required yearly targets are receiving promotions and/or pay rises they deserve. Line managers often hold colleagues back.
pros: Excellent work life balance, the best culture I have seen within a large organisation and great flexibility for colleagues. Lloyd’s Banking Group owns 100’s of companies, thus within the technology department you’ll never get bored. Lots to work on. The company offers great benefits such as; bonus, private medical care, concessionary mortgages, discounted current accounts, life insurance, Headspace app and one of my favourites international remote working in certain countries for 1 month a year. Lots of scope for training and gaining certifications, such as Google Cloud and Azure. Regular hackathons and offsite days to meet your team (as most the tech department is remote). Remote working for the majority of teams now across the bank. Unless an office is required for your role. Under great management since the new CEO joined the bank.
cons: The IRW programme doesn’t allow you to work abroad in many countries, for example India and Indonesia. It’s also a ‘reward’ your line manager must agree with. I think it’s a great idea allowing colleagues to work abroad remotely for 1 month per year, however I think the countries allowed needs to be expanded. And it should be applied for via HR and not via your line manager (aslong as your job is already remote, this wouldn’t work for branch staff for example). If you’ve a bad line manager, your pay and/or grade will stall for sure. Pay progression should again be managed more centrally.

pros: - The pay - I enjoyed my income enough for it to offset many drawbacks for a long time. - Working with many intelligent and dedicated colleagues who really wanted the best for customers. - Lloyds as an institution does broadly like the idea of making contributions to society and does excellent charitable work.
cons:
I had multiple reasons for leaving in the end but they generally linked to ethics. 

Any employee at the bank will have several goals/objectives but they'll be aware that only 1 or 2 will truly count. The financial and/or career stalling penalty for failing to achieving these annually will often far exceed the penalty for breaking rules / lacking integrity. How much you push your luck on this is at your discretion. 

At some point around 2015 onwards, there was an increasing shift in strategy from it being tolerably impersonal (let's face it - I never expected the banking sector to be hugs and kisses) to dehumanising. The best way I've come to describe working there is that it's what I imagine being in a cult is like - you somehow don't notice many of the things that make no sense until after you've left. 

By the time I left, the frequency I was being pressured to go outside my moral boundaries was very high. Hitting the core targets at any cost had facilitated a culture of power abuse not in isolated incidents but as the norm. Ironically, the people involved (due to their nature) often don't even seem to be serving the bank's interests now they've got where they need so just please themselves. 

Time and time again I saw inspiring people (often at more senior levels) sidelined in favour of autocrats who, in the absence/disregard of advice and relevant expertise, repeatedly created very peculiar strategies which would seem quite damaging to the bank. I've felt healthier than ever since resigning. My preference is that personalities like the Devil Wears Prada's Miranda Priestly and The Apprentice's Claude Littner stay on the TV.

advice: For the love of god, stop closing your ears. LISTEN! Get down to earth, stop seeing us as though we are ants and you are Gods. You are not Gods. Our job matters. Our job is important. We need more support, more trust, more KINDNESS, and less blame. Without us, without the role we do every single day, your job would either be 1000x harder or not even exist.
pros: Flex benefits - buying holiday, dental, private healthcare Some friendly colleagues Ability to change lives in small ways. Might sound like an exaggeration but you can be the reason someone can afford their food bill (or can't), or be the reason someone gets financial help, or other help when they desperately need it. Hours suit me.
cons: At the moment I am suffering mentally due to the taxing impact this company is having upon me. They pretend to listen to staff concerns - they do not. Management is completely disconnected. GI agents are seen as canon fodder - their feelings do not matter, their thoughts are irrelevant. I have tried emailing people in higher positions with suggestions as a result of my day-to-day role discoveries to find I get no answer, no response. Pointless surveys are sent out to fill in but not really acted upon. It's all talk, words - no action. Some people desperately want to work from home full time due to not being able to afford travel or are unwell but they are stopped from doing or have to fight to even though an overwhelming majority say they want to. There's talk about progression, but no appreciation for the majority of the colleagues doing a front line role. Their suggestions, ideas, their role is not valued. It's seen as the first rung on the ladder, rather than the reason this business even functions. We are made to feel as though abusive customers are noted and logged, when in reality they get paid to go away and paid despite abuse. To a colleague dealing with this it feels as though customers are being paid to be abusive. Colleagues are often targets and get absolutely no support from the business. If they can blame you - they will. If it can be your fault - it is. Pay is going up but not half as much as we deserve for the duties and complexities included in the role, often including that of a counselor (listening to some very distressing life events) and a mental health worker (dealing with extremely vulnerable, upset and upsetting customers), and a problem solver who can think instantly on the spot and handle complexities of varying degrees. All anyone can say is: "This is just how things are". It's stressful to call things out, stressful to attempt change. They say they crave change but only when it suits them and only when they decide. You are challenged and undermined, made to doubt reality, if you attempt to make changes they do not like. Mistakes or changes in processes from management that bring difficulty are dealt with mostly on the front line - if something goes wrong we're the first ones dealing with it but you can bet we'll also be the first ones to be blamed. We are the Whipping Boys of Lloyds. I honestly can't put into words the dissappointment I feel with this company and with my role at present.

advice: I've noticed more people have been leaving the bank with their great experience in toe. Having structure around 'future leaders' would be great to retain and nurture talent - this needs to be beyond the grad scheme and beyond a coffee with a random mentor. Also, make it easier to level out pay and reward those that work hard, smart and are loyal; often the jazzy new senior roles go to external candidates. I haven't met anyone that couldn't learn, be trained and/ or go on secondment in a new industry and come back with relevant experience for a leading role. Pay attention or your talent will ebb away.
pros: You'll be paid a good wage AND have a life AND enjoy your job (they shouldn't be at odds but many companies get this so out of balance). A lot of people have families so there is respect for that, equally if you don't have kids but have something you need to do that is also supported. If you show promise and state your desires for your career, there support to get you there but you have to be smart, reflect and navigate that.
cons: This is a massive old bank. That means risk appetite is low, meaning processes can be longer than in other businesses. But with that comes time to consider how to do it better and deliver great work too; you're not on a treadmill like in an agency. I have also noted that if you don't get feedback, frame your personal dev and ask for what you want, you can get trapped at your current level in the bank. It's a big place so the opportunities are there if you work for them. Pay at a peer level can also be out of kilter with performance, and it's a total pain to get it sorted for everyone involved. If it works out for you, the best way to solve that is move around/ up the ranks.

advice: Extremely poor management, if your face fits you'll go far, if it doesn't they'll get rid of you. Higher management don't listen when you're being bullied, they just move you to another branch hoping that the problem will go away. You have to commit to travelling within the 'Pool' temporary or permanent. They can move you at any time. They'll reimburse travel expenses if you're on cover but not if you're moved to a branch permanently so keep this in mind if parking is £5+ a day as the wage is already shocking. Massive responsibility and constantly on the look out for fraudulent transactions. Paid start time is 9am but they expect you to be there for 8:30am, often with the responsibility of door keys and opening up. You're paid until 4:30 but very very rarely leave at that time as they're currently (and have been for years) MASSIVELY MASSIVELY understaffed. Had to cancel social occasions such as family meals or miss outings with friends because I'm at work really late, only to be told by higher management  "Oh well, that's just the job you work in!". You cannot leave if you have an error, you must stop to find it. Workload was unbearable and if you're good at your job everything will fall onto you so you had to cram all jobs into a small space of time yet still expected to serve customers first. You cant do both. Systems are terrible, they never work properly, machines always breaking and always freezing/jamming causing delays during the day and at the end of the day. Avoid! Only good outcome are the friends I've made for life.

The lack of Due Diligence on the HBOS assets has been a widely publicised issue and although most of the write-downs were expected, it is slightly concerning that the board did not allow time to pick this up.

advice:
Sort out the complete lack of internal promotions in finance - otherwise the last remnants of experience/cumulative knowledge will leave.

Realise you can't have both the lean finance function and scrimp on investment in systems at the same time - one (or both!) need to change.

Try bringing in people to the leadership teams who are not like you. Lack of diversity means majority are alike in bullying approach to management.

Chronic lack of investment in systems means processes are becoming ever more likely to lead to errors. The result is that the people are so heavily leaned upon to sort things out. Sadly though, management have consistently reduced staff numbers in finance teams so team sizes are what they should be if there were state of the art systems in place.

Therefore work life balance is terrible for any half competent finance colleague. If they have a reasonable work life balance it means team members want them out of the way because they're more of a hindrance than a help.

Leadership of the business is becoming more aggressive, with the requirement to resolve issues inevitably left with staff - leaders just want to know who to blame if something goes wrong, and (more worryingly) who they will blame in the future if/when something goes wrong.

advice: Don’t micro manage your staff and treat them with some respect.  It is disgusting how you treat them.  And also remember staff get paid from 9am till 5pm.  Not 8:45 for your morning huddle / meetings

Constantly told by the bank there are no “targets” (even though the FCA abolished them), they call them “expectations” - and you have to hit them every month.  Sorry but anything you “have” to do monthly and work towards is a target! Dress it up how you want it’s a target!  Older members of staff are favoured over new ones and have first choice on days off and holiday booking.   Constantly lunch breaks missed due to inadequate time for appointments - lunch is for example 1-2pm. Wage is awful for the amount of work you are expected to do!  You have been warned.
