Calls are continuously coming In, no mid break, no time to write up notes, extremely rushed and management down your back if your not taking next call straight away.
Training is out of Belfast and not easy to get to if you don't drive.

pros: Good working environment and flexible working hours
cons: Changes happen too often, no career growth

pros: good work life balance, good people, supportive environment
cons: alot of governance, beaurucarcy , takes a while to climb the ladder

summary: Worst company I have ever worked for
advice: Hire managers who are good at being managers, not just people you are friendly with. If there are no targets, ensure the management are aware they shouldn't be pushing targets anyway.
pros: Moderate benefits and some nice colleagues if they allow you to work in a branch long enough to get to know people
cons: Management only care about targets although they will tell you there are no targets but you are still not doing well enough. No care for the morale of staff, just treat you like a machine, sending you to multiple branches all the time as it suits them. Poor pay for the work you are made to do and no support if you have a difficult customer, with the manager more often than not choosing the side of the customer as it is the easy option. Never congratulated on good achievements, only berated when you are thought you are not up to par with their standards. Made to do an apprenticeship so you can be paid less than other staff that do the same job as you even though you have coursework which you are not supported with.

pros: It’s a Good place to work
cons: Rate of pay is poor

summary: Very good company to work for, you get training and support to help you deliver good customer service.
advice: Managers can be supportive, however some  can favour favouritism in progression, my experience is keep a record of requests to managers, overall my manager has been supportive at times.
pros: Great company benefits, including full sick pay, great pension and medical private health care plan, the company have support available every day now, to help with customer service and the managers are supportive. Flexible shifts so this helps with child care.
cons: A lot to take in, servicing different brands and keeping up to date with the knowledge of bank products and terms n conditions and changes, can be challenging at times as you can feel under pressure, some days managers will pick up and add pressure on wrap times and Adhererance, which can go on to your performance record, overall if you like a challenging day and don’t mind change the jobs for you.

advice:
Performance and targets are there for a reason but when they're unachievable you should review them instead of blaming your staff for not achieving them. 

Stop telling your employees who tell you they are clinically depressed because of the way you treat them that If they don't take antidepressants it's their fault. Pills mask the problem that you refuse to stop causing. 

There is one simple way to keep your staff. Keep them happy and treat them like you care about them. Employees work hard for someone they have a good relationship with.
pros: Wages are ok, pay-for benefits are decent.
cons:
Targets are often unachievable which means frequent performance reviews and threats of job loss. This happens to stop the majority of workers from earning bonuses. 

Managers often ENCOURAGE staff to take anti-depression drugs to cope. 

Clique mentality. Who your friend is often dictates how far you will go. 

You are just a bum on a seat and nothing more. You're treated as a disposable asset and your strengths are overlooked as the company only focuses on your weaknesses. Don't expect to hear a good word about yourself working with them.

advice: Remember there's a client at the end of it and cut out some of the poor middle management.
pros: Large organisation with theoretically plenty of opportunity to move around. Being mediocre is absolutely fine which means the hours are pretty reasonable. The overall non-cash benefits are good.
cons: It's run by people who spend more time doing things to make themselves look good rather than what's right for the company. All of management had completely forgotten that the client should be at the heart of what they do and not someone just to make money out of. The performance review process and bonus payouts are completely opaque and depend on whether you are in favour at the time. Politics is more important than capability and your best chance of getting a promotion is just to sit in a role for a long time because if your face doesn't fit, you won't get promoted even if you are the top performer.

advice: Improve the structure of training for new employees and provide more support for the trainers.
pros: Bereavement Unit was a great department to work in, very much enjoyed my job. Great work-life balance and flexible hours: worked 35 hours a week, had complete choice over my start time and my manager actively encouraged us to always leave on time unless we'd requested overtime. Supportive management, and very friendly and helpful colleagues. Always opportunities to try something new/change roles.
cons: Targets were a little unrealistic as most people never reached them, however management didn't monitor performance particularly strictly. Training was very disorganised and had little to no struture.  Management were not particularly pro-active with providing further training even when it was desperately needed due to skill shortage.

summary: As bureaucratic as the USSR, more hierarchical than the Army, more British than Her Majesty
advice: Management needs being replaced. If the current management stays, please sort out the infrastructure and chop off the dead wood. Certain groups are worthless.
pros: Typical workload is maybe half than at similar institutions. If this is what you enjoy you can read novels at your desk and have 2-hour lunchbreaks.
cons:
Low workload generates a culture where unnecessary immaterial work is generated for the sake of filling up time. The staff are being constantly trained about the meaning of stakeholder management. Most of the middle management is inept and incapable of taking decisions. It repels talent and attracts (cannot get rid of) people close to retirement. The management sitting up in Halifax is a fiefdom of obtuseness.
It's also very adverse to non British people, apart from the facade of the CEO/CRO offices, if you are not British you won't be welcome.

summary: AWFUL AWFUL AWFUL AWFUL AWFUL AWFUL
advice: Nothing that I cold comment on in writing.
pros: Big company, big company benefits
cons:
Hugely corporate which you might expect but management, certainly in recent times, only looking to manage people out without having to pay redundancy. I submitted harrassment complaint against a local director. Not interested in any views unless they agree with the company line. Management often harrass and bully resulting in many people being off sick, often long term , with stress.
May have been good company to work for years ago but I do not have a single positive thing to say other than the people at branch level were fine but higher up the line I have nothing good to offer.
I was often asked to work in a highly unprofessional manner and do things which were definately unethical and improper and was not at all surprised when they were reported as the biggest culprit in the PPI misselling scandal.

advice: Change your old computers , time has moved forward but your Leeds branch is stuck in Stone Age with your flintstones crew.....I've seen the flintstones advert but this a step to far!! Start by Changing your classroom coach, Foxtrot Alpha Zulu.
pros:
Decent pay and on time 
Free coffees and plenty of free water 
Nice canteen facilities with loads of microwaves 
Cheap Starbucks 
Decent cash back offers on staff account
cons:
Bad management system 
If you dare talk back to your TM or criticise anything even the slow old rusty machines you're good as gone immediately or bullied out of the place slowly but surely.
They tell you in training if you have trouble with anything at work or outside work then they will help you. The truth of the matter is, if you go to them with any of your problems then they will consider you as a problem and start counting your days......

summary: Loyalty to the business doesn't pay
advice: Be more approachable and personal with the colleagues in your team; get to know them, spend some time with them, listen to them. 121 and support meetings are supposed to be a balanced conversation, not just the Manager talking all the time!
pros: LBG try to promote and encourage employees to focus on training and development. Also have a good benefit and reward package.
cons: Although the business say they value their employees and have the right people in the roles, some of the management team do not have the personal skills to be supporting colleagues, they pressure the work on so much that you do not have time for training and development. They treat you as a number, not a valued colleague.

summary: Large but Inclusive and Caring Company
advice: Keep the positive focus on your people and they will do the right thing for your customers.
pros:
Lots of communication from senior leadership and a clear vision and strategy.
Good employee benefits which are available immediately to all staff.
A caring culture with lots of attention to colleague engagement and satisfaction.
An embedded ethos of doing the right thing for customers above and beyond the profit motive.
cons:
Systems and processes are a bit creaky with manual workarounds required to make some things work.
Some people have been in the business for decades which can lead to it being a bit inwardly focused. But they care.
Not the most dynamic business, preferring tried and tested to bold and innovative.

summary: UK focussed bank with many technological, cultural and behavioural issues that it is making some progress on
advice:
Resolve the contraints that you place on employees  - trust more, reward on competence and potential 
Change the culture so it is more adult to adult - rather than parent child
pros:
You are paid on time, there is a great resiliance within the workforce to do a good job despite the constraints placed upon them. Some great people that make things happen for customers and colleagues.  

Good range of policies and salaries are okay - however application of policy by management and local practices diminish the intent of the organisation
cons:
If you want to deliver you will constantly face issues with technology, governance and a lack of consistent  leadership from collegaues below the Group Exec. 

Line Managers and colleagues are not trusted to do a good job - lots of micro management and reporting - so train leaders to lead, assess their ability to lead and trust them to get on with it! 

Some leaders talk a good game but do not follow through with tangible activity

advice: Continue the good work to streamline processes - establish a process ownership function to guard against individual teams adding layers of customised process otherwise it'll turn into a bird's nest again. Eliminate duplication of PM process responsibility (have 1 IT PM, not one per supply area). Build flexibility into the Performance Management process so that colleagues on 'unique' assignments don't have to tick all the boxes as if they've been operating in formation like Cybermen.
pros:
Great team spirit - surrounded by capable colleagues who just get on with it.
Good development opportunities/support.
Opportunities to work on a variety of assignment types (but make your preferences known).
Good support from Line Management.
Good working environment (quality of offices and locations)
cons:
Historically knee-deep in process - frustrating, although recognised and action is being taken.
Obsession with cost cutting - process must surely cost more to operate than it saves.
If you don't make your ambitions clear, your next assignment is determined lottery-fashion.
Performance management is done 'by numbers' - you have to tick all the boxes whether they truly add value or not - fail to do so and you're an easy target.

advice: Listen to staff, just because people are paid less it doesn't mean their ideas are any less relevant
pros: Diverse opportunities available along with steadily improving financial prospects.  It's very hard to make the leap to higher bands but once made that step there are good opportunities. Work life balance is encouraged with flexible hours available.  The CEO seems to be doing a good job considering how much of a mess the company has been.
cons: Salary is well below being market competitive, very hard to progress to higher levels through hard work only - you have to really butter up the current management and become part of their favoured group.  The companies systems and processes would look old in the mid-80's.

advice: My Senior management had been at the bank for 20+ years and was quite frankly jaded. I would refer to him as an 'incumbant' and if I was a permanent employee I would look to move into another team asap.  He was nice enough but I felt he was probably one of the members of senior management to be resisting  the organisational change occurring in Lloyds. No advice just an observation. The management landscape in the next 10-20 years will hopefully be me diverse and engaged in change.
pros: Scope to explore the bank and and get involved in a wide variety of projects. There isn't really a ceiling to the number of opportunities available if you are keen to make the most of them. Also, I was able to work from home twice a week and my team were super helpful in helping me settling in and learning the ropes.
cons: This depends on your expectations and ability to communicate. My expectations were met and I had a good relationship with my team so there weren't really any Cons. I was sad to leave.

summary: Supports Mental Health UK....unless it involves their actual staff
advice: Instead of talking about how much you support Mental Health for your staff, actually do something about it.  A free subscription to the Headspace app means nothing when your staff are overworked and stressed.
pros: Fellow staff members, I've met some of the best people working here. Highly skilled, motivated, funny. Just a shame most of them get grinded down to a shadow of themselves by the business.
cons:
Management seem obsessed with reducing staff levels of teams to the lowest they can possibly run at. Resulting in increased stress and workload for the remaining staff.

Management have no understanding of what work-life balance is and will expect you to work excessive hours to hit targets.

summary: Nice people, but huge amount of burocracy & politics makes everything but impossible real action & meritocracy
advice: Need to really get all senior management with them and ensure this becomes a really One Bank
pros:
Nice face of banking, relationship oriented
People are relatively open to collaboration
cons:
Huge politics (decision making biased by agendas)
Mediocrity of senior management (not fact-based, not high caliber)
Execution drawn back by burocracy (lots of committees, paperwork, rules & policies,...)
Hierarchy is overwhelming
Cultural clash between top management (new, from Santander) and incumbent senior management (old LTSB/HBOS school... or new but alien to the bank ways)... big problem
Absence of meritocracy (families, politics, fake non-factual evaluations, ...)
Pays very badly (does not update salaries other than for CPI... does not matter how much more responsibility or promotion you get)

advice: Look after your established employees they will look after your new employees and you will retain the best and they will pass on their experience. Get rid of lazy managers who pretend to do a good job in front of higher managers at the expense of consultants!weed them out you know who they are
pros: Job security worked with some great people.some good benefits.time given for medical breaks that's it for me never really used any of the other benefits seemed like token gestures good save as you earn schemes
cons: Some managers had ideas above themselves never really pulled there weight.rubbish performance reviews used as an excuse not to get a wage rise.struggled to book holidays you did the job of 4 people but were paid less then market rate.more and more work for less pay. Very low morale managers did not want to acknowledge this.high turnover of staff because of pay scale you are just a number in a high corporate company and if your face fits and suck up or know the right people the sky is the limit!

summary: A fast paced with much to learn
advice: Structure the learning process for old and new staff (Inc contractors) to get the best out of everyone. It's a big establishment with a lot to learn so empower everyone with more knowledge in order to do well.
pros:
Friendly environment with a strong focus on improving customer satisfaction.  
Flexible working with option to work from home on occasion.
cons:
Intense and tough screening/vetting process to get through after offer was made. 
Long teleconference meetings that overlap mean you have to become a multitasking genius to get all the tasks done at the same time. 
Hard to get even basic information and training to get simple tasks done. Left to your own devices to learn everything on the job.

advice: You should get it together.
pros:
Business is set up well due to the fact it's such a large entity and as such everything has a running process. 

Learning materials are always in reach.
cons:
Poor management the place is a bureaucracy, unless you brown nose you're not getting any sort of progression regardless of the merits of your work. 

Again credit isn't given where it's due. Many colleagues within the department are lazy and are less than motivated in bringing about the best business outcome for Llyods and clients. 

If the FCA were to probe I'm sure there would be some misgivings maybe not gross but definitely not upto scratch. And given the size and reputation of the company it's not good enough. The amount of complaints received from customers was unbelievable. When the business makes serious errors themselves it just makes your job that much harder. You're not going to get the best out of your employees in those conditions. Constant issues and failures by the business which could have been avoided if the employees themselves worked up to scratch and management were competent.

Few of the management are competent the vast majority have a napoleon complex and power trip. 

I really enjoyed the work itself it was really interesting but Lloyd's made me loathe being there.

advice: Management need to lose their misguided god like status and treat colleagues with respect. When colleagues are sitting at their desk in tears after a discussion record with a manager or worse still walking out because of the constant hounding you have to accept that there is something very very wrong with the working environment. And it's 100% managers and their inflated egos
pros: Can make decent money if you can tolerate the poor management
cons:
Managers treat you like kids, really toxic environment. Managers are on your back every minute of every day. I worked in a few depts and found the management in the Opal Crew Belfast to be the worst. They don't care about customers or employees- they are just mini hitlers. Some of the women managers in particular are so unapproachable and hung up on their own self importance. 
So if you decide to work there prepare yourself to be micro-managed to within an inch of your own sanity. Managers are on your back 24/7- you don't get a chance to breathe between calls and managers sit looking for things they feel you did wrong. And while colleagues on the phone don't get a breather managers sit there freely chatting away amongst themselves about everything non work related they want to.

summary: Everything you would expect and nothing more
advice: If you want to change a culture then rather than pick the most bland statements from the hr handbook and ask for bottom up input on how to create it, try and set culture from the top.
pros: All the things that come with a large company.  Big pension, excellent work life balance if desired, job security through heavily unionised workforce and an incredibly resilient brand in an industry with highly resilient clients.  Opportunities to move around the firm if desired.
cons: A huge, in-agile tanker filled with mediocre employees who (in the Commercial Bank) get paid too well.  Lack of any strategy, direction or drive below the level of the CEO (who is a very impressive, although not particularly human character) resulting a lot of bumbling corporate types looking busy but not really achieving anything.  No identifiable culture to speak of besides 'nice'.  If you are driven and want to affect meaningful change then stay clear - you might upset the applecart and you may be psychologically damaged depending on how long you stay.

advice: Please train your Ops Managers in the hopes you retain staff moving forward
pros: Excellent packages available if you are happy to be tied in to the company.  Training given for regulation purposes is easy to access.  Promotion is available to a certain extent but is fragmented  on the whole.
cons: Middle management is poor with very little understanding of the need for interpersonal skills required for such positions which in my experience has caused resentment within the department this led to my resignation even though higher management were great to work with. Work life balance has no place within the department I worked in and total discrimination against colleagues who wished to take leave during the school holidays as priority always given to the colleagues who had children no consideration of staff family units that don't fit the norm.  Very difficult to get annual leave requests passed without a fight.  Colleagues underpaid for the role they perform and work load is very high in a very stressful target driven environment most people stressed and demotivated.

summary: Job security not as good as it used to be, pay is average
advice: Stop the contraction.  Let people find their feet for a few years.
pros: It’s a big company so you can move around.  They are very big on regular performance reviews and have a very strict but simple rating system.
cons:
It’s a bank that is contracting in size and has been for ten years.  Expect to have to go through what they call ‘preferencing’ every 18 months where if you are not placed in one of the fewer vacancies they have, you’ll get booted.  

They have the worst, most unreliable, clunky old systems I have ever used.  Minimal investment in this area results in many frantic incident calls and meetings most days of the week.  

They are also really into positive discrimination - they have targets to promote women before men likewise with ethnically challenged people, so if you’re an able bodied white straight male, it definitely isn’t the company for you but to be honest you wouldn’t get a job with them anyway.

advice: Be realistic, stop the sales and actually care about the customers.
pros: Can the chance to help people with there day to day finances and great for relationship building skills
cons: Managers are out of touch with job role, all about quantity and pushing complex needs! If you dont do a loan or home insurance expect to get it in the ear. You are compared to other colleagues which was meant to be stopped years ago when targets were scrapped however managers still write down what you have done. Expect phrases from management going along the lines of 'do a loan for a driveway cause they have good CAPS. CAPS is the risk rating from the bank. All they want is for you to sell. You can really help someone with  savings getting them more interest but you will get no credit cause you havent sold anything. For the money it is really not worth it and with current cuts in jobs there is no long term plans. The management is also awful in the bank.

advice: If you want staff you be equipped to do their jobs effectively, they need to be trained properly not just given a week crash course, and support needs to be available  at all times not just Monday to Friday 9-5
pros: Grate benefits, flexible working hours, good personal development opportunities, good atmosphere, people driven, opportunities to move department within the business,
cons: Promotions are give to people who are friends with the management, not always on merit, management try to you to service as many different departments as possible but do not give the correct support or training need, they just throw you into the deep and think it will work,

summary: Lovely people make this a great place to work - if you can put up with old tech and broken process
advice: Get rid of all the janky process and allow your amazing staff to shine!
pros:
Really dedicated and brilliant staff who have the customers best interests at heart.
Interesting projects, labs, guilds and stuff going on. If you're interested in a specialism you're encouraged to explore it and make it part of your job.
Excellent work/life balance
cons:
Old tech, forced to use a PC to check email, cruddy old intranet and internal systems kind of get you down.
Lack of direction and buy-in from management. Everything always changing and in flux - desks, lockers, etc.
Limited external training and no budget to attend conferences.

advice: Don't be so easily manipulated by unprofessional and career hungry individuals.
pros: Good company benefits and good location
cons:
Management changed team manager on the back of some very poor advice and manipulated information, to bring in an extremely aggressive and unprofessional manager. Life became utterly unbearable under the new manager leading to 3 out of a team of 8 leaving within 6 months.

Although management realised their mistake and replaced the manager after 6 months, it was incredible that such a bad error of judgement was displayed with no regard for the wellbeing of employees, as well as thoroughly destroying the career and credibility of the previous manager who was excellent, professional, well liked and very capable. Bizarre decision making.

advice:
Get rid of the snowflake thinkers who came up with these ideas and who think that by saying we're changing things mean they happen over night and who then have a tantrum when it doesn't happen.

You've lost a lot of knowledge and experts with idiotic thinking and decisions.
pros: Overall Package and Benefits are better than others.
cons: New ways of working in I.T. haven't been properly thought through before implementing and too many changes being implemented at once - two major ones are failing miserably with a supplier failing to deliver any quality service at all, resulting in lots of people in IT looking to leave and moral is at an all time low.

advice: Keep caring about staff
pros:
Lloyds really care about their staff and try to retain as many as possible. There’s a huge proportion who have been there for 10+ years.

The best benefit package I have seen from any employer I’ve worked for.

Good holiday allowance, generous pension with large contribution from Lloyds, 4% of salary as extra cash each month you can keep or buy additional benefits like increased medical care/more holidays/dental. Really good salaries especially for people in the earlier stages of their careers.
cons:
Archaic processes that are over complicated 
Some technology is outdated
Hard to keep up with what’s going on sometimes
Good working hours but could offer more flexibility like flexi time or a 9 day fortnight

summary: Poor training, paradoxical targets and micromanagement.
advice: If customer service is actually top of their agenda then start focusing on customer service properly with the abolishment of sales targets. Start supporting new entrants as much as existing roles.
pros: Good Salary, Friendly people (excluding management), starting to focus on customer service and regain the trust of customers.
cons: Inflexible working hours, bureaucratic and micromanagement yet poor support of new entrants. The targets the company has, encompasses both sales targets with excellent customer service. However, the 'service' side is only a front for the hidden agenda of sell, sell, sell focused on by management, a complete paradoxical situation. Also Lloyds Bank places BANS on peoples progression with 'placement lock' which is unbelievable.

advice: Actually listen to your colleague opinions from the results of the surveys, don't just listen to managerial interpretations on what the verbatim means.
pros:
Good benefits - staff mortgage, colleague annual bonus, free shares etc which keeps you loyal to the wider business.
Culture good at times, in regards to fun activities only.
cons:
Culture - there's a lot of unhappy colleagues who stay as they feel trapped with colleague mortgage etc.
Very hierarchical management structure. If your face doesn't fit, you've no chance of progressing.
Agile working policies in place -fine for management to have but not for the lower level colleagues.
Bullying managers in place who will make life difficult for you, higher management aware & do nothing about it.

advice:
Start treating your staff fairly and equally.
Have a bit of compassion, put yourself in shoes of your staff. 
Stop making false promises and be honest!
Customers comes first but stop making staff feel worthless.
pros: Benefits. Bank holidays off,  good deals (products)
cons:
Company only cares about profit. It's not Customer Service it's SALES, SALES, SALES. They don't care how did you help customer unless you'll help them selling Mortgage or Loans. 

Management will promise you training or progress only to keep you in branch. Won't happen unless you're a man.

Some customers are nice some will treat you terribly, some will spit at you or abuse you. Some managers won't do anything about it!

Might be a good job for people that are just leaving school otherwise think twice before joining. You'll be rushed all the time, stressed and the only thing that matters is sales.

Gets worst and worst with every month.

advice: Please update IT hardware in branches and do something meaningful to resolve our slow, unreliable IT systems - they're an embarrassment. Furthermore, value the qualifications of your staff - it's not right to underpay someone with a university education.
pros: Decent work-life balance. There are some good benefits to working here - including: share options; a reasonable pension; health insurance and dental cover.
cons: Limited opportunities for career progression. IT services are antiquated and notoriously slow and unreliable. Pay is low - I was particularly upset to be given no more than an entry level salary when I joined the company, despite having 2 good degrees to my name and some years in the workforce before changing careers.

summary: Good for British, terrible for foreigners
advice: Change immediately or just watch most of your people leave
pros:
- Decent salary according to market standards
- Work-life balance
cons:
I had to leave because during pandemic Lloyds treated us unfairly and they didn't care about our mental health.
- They fired 3000 people giving them really short notice.
- They cut bonuses, but not for all of us.
- No career progression. They don't promote people fairly.
- They say they want diversity but they didn't let foreigners work from their home country. A few more senior colleagues though spent months abroad without any issue. If you are non British and you want some flexibility, at least for short term, don't choose Lloyds.

Also, work is so repetitive and you cannot make a difference in there. Stakeholders never accept yours solutions and your work is wasted. If you want bureaucracy and slow progression choose Lloyds. Otherwise, stay away!

summary: Started good, and consistently got worse
advice: Quit the micro-managing, and give employees the freedom to actually do their job
pros: Some really great people there, Get to start at 9, and finish at 5, and erm... that's about it
cons: I work within Business Banking Direct, and the place has steadily deteriorated from a telephone based relationship management position, to a call centre. Though they pay lip service to things like customer service, the reality is that you're pushed to sell as much to each customer, to turn a complaint into a sales call. The incessant micro-managing and clique-y nature of senior management means progression is VERY difficult, unless you happen to be quite cosy with the team leaders or the senior management... real sad given the amount of natural talent in that place.

advice: Stop paying more for average contractors than you do for talented permanent staff, and review the policy of shuffling the deck rather than actually dealing with underperformance.
pros: I'm given a huge amount of freedom to work in the way that I want to, my opinions are trusted, my suggestions acted upon, and my job feels more like a hobby than a chore.
cons: People who are inept at their jobs never leave, they just move from team to team, intermittently dragging down the average IQ until they inevitably take part in the next round of musical chairs. This just takes up space that could be used to employ talented people instead.

advice: Rethink the group’s values as it’s demoralising when you see they are not upheld.
pros:
I have to write a minimum of 5 words but there’s only two pros I can think of: 
Pay
Agile working
cons:
A lot of noise is made about the group’s values but they are not upheld internally - same with their support for mental health U.K; a lot of noise is made but not much is done to support colleagues going through a (work related) mental health crisis, yes there is EAP but previous employers I’ve worked for also offered this; LBG are not offering anything more in this regard.
Cliques 
Unreasonable expectations 
Not being taken seriously when speaking up on issues such as bullying 
It’s a dog eat dog mentally here
Possibly the worst place I’ve ever worked

summary: An Executive struggling to run a business of this size
advice: The business is about its customers and staff, not about the returns for the Senior Executive. Stop using Branded consultancies to do their job, like McKinsey and BCG, understand your customers, build a strategy for each sector, and empower the best people you have to execute it.
pros: In the main, the frontline staff care about the customers, and each other. The customers try and have a relationship with the Bank, and there are a lot of management trying to do the right thing.
cons: Ineffective Executive, self centred, material lack of Strategic Direction, similar in Leadership. They have created a fear culture, where people are afraid to challenge, and up and down the line communication is non existent.

summary: Okay.... Digital Arm is run by non experience and politically inlcided people
advice: Once you have hired smart people from outside, let them do their work and run the show. Be there as a guide and mentor rather than hiring them and then tell them how you would have been running it all your life and they are not supposed to change it.
pros: Overall company is moving in the right direction, there is a will to do something better for customer and employees.
cons: However, Top-level people (in their late 50s) owning the Digital arm are very politically inclined. They don't understand the digital world but they pretend as if they invented it and they own the whole company and so nothing goes ahead if it does not suit their personal agenda.

advice:
Prevent further eroding of skill-base.
Impose a single language standard within the Company, whether that be Hindi or English.
Stop the Company from being seen as a 'nursery' for competitors to use to head-hunt top staff.
Encourage employment of female technical staff.
pros: Solid market performer. It isn't Barclays.
cons:

summary: Failure to practice what they preach re. mental health
advice: Have a dedicated mental health support policy, and stop using a policy that threatens dismissal for ill health, especially when the employee demonstrates a determination to get well and return to work. Enforce completion of diversity and inclusion training by line managers: 100% compliance, no exceptions. Make flexible working accessible for ALL employees, in ALL functions and roles. Managers / directors seem to bend over backwards to make it work for mothers, but everyone else is declined part-time working due to "business requirements". Better monitoring of performance management, ensuring new-to-role employees and those with health issues are not given a "developing performer" rating unless there really are issues with their performance on the days they are in work.
pros: A major U.K. employer in Finance, paying good salaries, and with the opportunity to earn an annual bonus, share save scheme, staff mortgage rate and other benefits.
cons:
Based on personal experience. 1 in 4 people suffer a mental health problem such as anxiety or depression at some point in their lives. Lloyds employs tens of thousands of people, so that's a lot of people who might be struggling. Yet despite having a policy of inclusion and support of people with disabilities, including a "guaranteed interview" policy for applicants with a history of disability such as mental health issues, in reality Lloyds are far from supportive or inclusive. 

Firstly, their attendance policy is unrealistic and punitive for anyone with a long-term health issue, such as anxiety or depression, even though that person may be an excellent employee who does their utmost to be in work and get well. Less than 98% attendance - that's 5 days sick a year for a 9-5 Mon-Fri employee - quickly leads to you being under an attendance review policy that, far from support the employee, puts pressure on you to be in work 98% of the time, and threatens you with dismissal within a short period of time. Hardly conducive to rebuilding and maintaining mental health. 

Their flexible working policy is the opposite of flexible, unless you're a mother returning from maternity leave. So even though you could be a highly-productive and valuable part-time employee, and maintain your health working fewer than 35hrs a week, you are forced to stay full-time, so then your chances of being successful at meeting the attendance requirements of a full-time role are slim, and you're set up to fail.

To add insult to injury, despite the performance management policy supposedly a) being totally separate from any attendance policy, and b) on paper enabling anyone to get rated as "Good", no matter how long they've been in the role or their attendance, in reality anything less than full attendance and 6+ months experience in a role will see you labelled as "Developing". More than two quarters in a row at this rating means you're then put under a performance management process, on top of the attendance management process. 

The total lack of empathy on the part of HR employees, policies that are utterly unsuited to those with the mental health issues that 1 in 4 of us will suffer in our lives (they seem to have been written for non-mental-health issues, maybe a broken leg or cancer), and line managers who can get away with claiming completion of "diversity and inclusion training" without actually doing it, so are totally uneducated and unprepared to deal with anyone with depression / anxiety, all mean that great employees end up leaving, with their mental health worse than when they first became unwell. In the 21st century this is not just sad, it's a disgrace.

advice: Sending your line managers to a short course on mental health first aid does not make them experts and they should not act as if they are. They should listen to their colleagues and not push them into changing medication and undergoing counselling if they are not at a point where they feel they are capable of this or if it's necessary.  Medication changes are incredibly serious and not to be dictated by a manager purely because they want you back at work asap. Managers should also be understanding that when a plan is created and the colleague has undertaken most of the actions besides maybe a couple, to not make them feel guilty or as if they're having a massive go at them as this is counterproductive to their recovery. A huge symptom of many mental health illnesses is memory issues. Some colleagues off sick with mental health reasons are struggling to find a reason to stay alive, so a manager having a go at them for forgetting to fill out a form really isn't part of the bigger picture. There is a matter of duty of care that needs to be taken into consideration.

advice: Please start treating frontline staff like people instead of cattle. There's a mental health crisis going on within Lloyds due to the strict toxic work culture you've created and enabled. You're stuck in the 20th century while the rest of the professional world is moving on. Your staff turnover rates alone should give you a hint. Please take on feedback and actually listen and do something about grievances. cons:
1. Toxic work culture 
- talk of mental health, videos and emails about it but basically zero support is provided when someone actually needs it. Instead the approach taken by management is of intimidation, pressure, guilt-tripping and invasive questioning. You wouldn't believe how many people have left because of this. The staff turnover is abysmal. 
The only thing they'll say is they are here to support you but they have no idea how to do that. They'll give you the standard speech and then tell you to contact the in-house mental health advisors, whether that's what is right for your situation or not. 
- they have no understanding of the impact of racist abuse many advisors receive over the phones. The amount of times I've seen it being brushed away is crazy. The approach of "tell the customer you'll speak as slow as they want" when the customer is spewing racist bile over you is so damaging. Again, talk of support, inclusivity and diversity is there, but the reality is that no one's educated in these areas to actually know how to support someone going through this day after day. 
- ever changing lower management. I must've had 4 managers in less than 5 months because of the constant changes. There's no stability, no proper planning, no understanding of the impact on employees. 
- feedback is not taken aboard by upper management no matter how many surveys they get you to fill. They'll always come back with "don't have the budget for this right now", while people keep leaving and no one is hired to replace them. The extreme work load will keep getting divided between those who are left and all of the suggestions, feedback, etc. will fall on deaf ears.
- have heard from team mates of managers bullying, singling out and intimidating colleagues for speaking up or calling them out on unprofessionalism.

2. No recognition
- you can work like crazy, take on multiple projects, collaborate with departments and do way beyond your job title, but there's barely any recognition, and there's certainly no progression. No matter how much you show that you've gone beyond and are eager to progress, internal role selections seem extremely biased and are usually going to people already known to the hiring managers or within their own departments. 
- you have to keep chasing hiring managers to provide some kind of feedback at least after a declined application or interview. Some managers don't even bother to respond. 
- the bonus is pathetic honestly. There's no bonus this year at all despite the hard work employees have put in throughout the Covid crisis and even though Lloyds has been in profit. The bonus last year wasn't worth talking about either. 

3. The timings and the shift pattern are horrendous. Half of your health issues will start just because planning doesn't care and will most likely schedule you for an early morning start after late night finish.

My mental health had never suffered so badly until working at Lloyds. It went from bad to worse, to the point that I had multiple breakdowns and was a jittery anxious wreck. Your mind will grow stagnant even if you push yourself to take on additional projects. You'll feel burn-out all the time. 

I only had one amazing manager who was always supportive and a real gem. The rest are either unfeeling robots or extremely uneducated on how to support their team members through a mental health crisis. 
Usually the lower management's hands are tied because the upper management really, really don't care about frontline staff and their ordeals.

The relief I felt after handing in my notice was immense. And the progressive culture shock of my new work place really opened my eyes to how backward Lloyds' approach is and how little they care for their junior staff members.
