summary: Good structured placement with fair pay.
advice: Work on developing internal staff rather than sending too much work overseas. Bringing in fresh ideas from graduates will drive the business forward.
pros: Good friendly relaxed work environment. Excellent development opportunities and good feedback from management regarding work. As an industrial placement student the pay was slightly above par with other company's. The industrial placement scheme itself was well run and structured. It had clear goals and allowed students to develop and also gain additional skills which would then become useful for returning to university.
cons: Unsure job future due to the large amount of off shoring going on in the IT areas of the company. Some areas of the business could so with some new fresh ideas. IT placements and graduates were reduced due to offshoring so less opportunities for new staff to come in.

advice: Treat you staff better instead of just instilling values that the employees have to the business and company how about instilling values that the company should view on its employee dont just value the customer value employees dont just class them as a number show understanding and empathy and support to employees give them a chance.  Easy formula happy employees = happy workers = excellent service= happy customer=retention and good word of mouth= more business= more £££££££££££.    A happy customer may tell 1 in 10 people but unhappy customer will tell at least 8 out of 10.  So which is is LBG  a preference of looaing 8 customers or gaining 1?  By the way warning to all a GRIEVANCE has been put to a SENIOR MANAGER JASON WILLIAMS OF CARDIFF GATE  I believe by customer advisers that says it all.
pros: Pay but bear in mind it goog in 1st 2 years but hardly anything after that get penalised for being at the higher rate in your level you only get 1% pay rise but on a lower pay can get 5% no fair for the higher performer and lonevity and loyaly of employment.  I enjoyed my role and providing a high standard of customer service but did not enjoy working for the company
cons: The company is not interested in their employers.  They have a sickness poliy in place so rigid and dont be deceived its not there for the support of employres its in place to get you out of tge business when they dont want you there anymore.  Their retention is appauling.  They want staff of short service.  They dpnt want the long servicing loyal employees because we cost to much or we have had reasonable adjustments to our hours and are part time mums.  All they wanr is students  who are desperate for the monry that they will work all the unsociable hours going.  Your expected not to have a life but to work til 10 at night and 6 out of 8 shifts on a weekend out of just 4 weekends getting time off is virtually impossible.  They are clicky its all about your face fitting and networking.

summary: Good pay, not so good work
advice:
Processes really do need to be tightened up, as a lot of the methods of dealing with queries and complaints are horrendously inefficient and cause more complaints because of that.
Calls in regards to mortgages or anything more complex than standard banking enquiries (which is only what we were trained in) should be routed through IVR and not come through to bank accounts, as we have no clue what an investment plan or insurance premiums are, so not very efficient there either.
Ease up on after call work, I understand you need to have people answering phones quickly, but 3 seconds is a joke.
You need to be aware of people who would be better suited to other positions and offer them progression or they will get frustrated and leave.
pros:
Good hourly rate, bonuses were nice to have too. Some calls with customers were rewarding but not very often. Nice time off the phone also reasonably frequently while on shift and paid break. Search database for help on processes is really good, often if you didn't know something you could just search on that using keywords.
If you need good cash in short period then it's great, but full timers seem depressed and bored.
cons:
Systems were constantly crashing and no fixes are ever really introduced, you're given "workarounds" which usually means putting customer on hold and restarting your systems. This rarely ever fixed anything. 
Complaints process is clunky and inconvenient, usually lasting around 30-40 minutes due to the fact you need to check with a manager after explaining situation to customer only for manager to tell you to do something different and then rinse and repeat until customer accepts resolution or gets frustrated and hangs up. very limited to what we could do to resolve complaints and when you escalated it to "specialist team" they told you to relay things to customer instead of speaking to them directly which adds another 20 minutes to call.
Expected to do the manager's work for them when you work on your personal development plan. You don't get any time off the phone to do this and i suppose you're expected to do this in the 3 seconds you get between calls... not happening.
Managers are frequently absent on the floor when you need support, often going to a managers meeting so that ALL managers are gone from the floor and one person is put on a help phone for the whole floor, not efficient.
Most people there are quite relaxed, as they don't often like the job any more than you do. This can sometimes extend to managers, some are a little too relaxed to offer anything other than standard advice that often doesn't resolve the situation.
You have to choose between doing the job well or doing the job right, as you're not allowed to use the after call time to add notes to a customers account that could potentially help out the next colleague that takes the customer or a branch colleague who gets a visit from that customer. Constantly told to keep your after call work to less than 20 seconds, if not you get comments.
Often manager's will wander around or talk with each other about personal matters while you're sitting taking call after call with a 3 second break in between and only get support once the call abandonment rate in the queue is too high.
Told that you must work in same shifts for at least 12 months after start date before being able to change shifts to different times, which was not true as this is possible with a manager that finds the time to help you. However, after getting these shifts changed there is no leeway for another 6 months.
Promises of rapid advancement and promotion opportunities in training but when you're actually on the floor you just have to really plod along and never really get a second glance. Never offered to move departments either, seems like you have to be there for 3+ years before that's an option.
You're only really there to repeat what's on a screen, so if you like creative thinking and not feeling like you're repeating yourself over and over again ("no you can't change your address over the phone at this time, no you can't add a new payment recipient, no even if it is very important that's the policy we have, yes you can speak to a manager but they'll tell you the same).

summary: A strong business but can neglect it's staff
advice: Look after your staff more. Yes, it's important to keep the business modern and adapt to changes, but leaving so many in constant threat of their jobs causes incredible amounts of stress and upset. Staff simply cannot do their jobs properly in those circumstances and they become disloyal to the business.
pros:
- Particularly after the banking issues a few years back, Lloyds has a clear plan of where it wants to be and how it's getting there. As such, the business is doing well for itself.

- There's a big focus on diversity, with networks for minority groups and loads of support and opportunities available for those wanting to take it up

- The company has quite clear structures and processes, such as performance management, so you know what to expect and it's usually clear how things work

- The business was spending a lot of money on modernising systems
cons:
- The business is moving so fast, that things often change too fast and staff were messed around or given conflicting direction 

- As an example, in branch, we went through job restructures three times in 2 years, on each occasion, having to reapply for our jobs or face redundancy. One one occasion, we were told of this within a month of completing the last restructure. 

This caused huge stress to those at risk of losing their jobs.

It disrupted their work, as you were having to focus on reapplying instead of you day to day work. It disrupted other colleagues who were affected by your lack of focus, and by frequent management changes.

- Messages from the top were somewhat distorted on the way down. Sales targets may have gone out the window a few years back, but staff were still pushed to sell a minimum number of products to prove their competence or be threatened with extra training and 'support', with the possibility of it leading to disciplinary.

- The changes to the way customers use branches means there's less staffing in branches - staff are required to carry out extra roles and increasing pressure on them.

- Fewer branch roles means less opportunities to progress in your career.

- Poor work life balance in branch - those working till the end of the day were just expected to stay until things were done, regardless of how late it could get. Claiming time back, particularly as a manager, was difficult if not impossible.

advice: Be more transparent with graduate. Listen to what they are interested in more.
pros:
Good exposure to different parts of the bank. 
- Good employee wellbeing
- Fairly good working hours (9-5) depending on your stream.
cons:
You have to stay for two years after the end of the graduate scheme in order to not owe them any money. If you leave at the end of the two years, you owe them the money for the qualification you must take during the scheme, which they aren't transparent about from the beginning. 
- There isn't much say in the rotations you do.

pros:
- Transition to working from home meant better work-life balance 
-Great starting job which will open opportunities internally and externally 
- Overtime when available 
- Progression opportunities available but you must actively seek them 
- 4% of your wage extra taken in any way you choose e.g. extra holidays, health insurance or as cash etc.
- Sharematch
- Very good pension scheme
cons:
- Experience is very manager dependent 
- Lack of communication from bottom down 
- Call centre role very demanding in terms of expectations - very highly monitored i.e. adherence, after call work etc.
- Your voice can often feel unheard

advice: Nothing to say just be the same.
pros: A place which helps us to grow in terms of job and a really good work environment to work in. Employees are given the rights to speak for their rights and gives importance to our opinions.
cons: Only thing I would say is the shift timings were not helping me, as I stay in kirkcaldy and had to commute to work every evening from kirkcaldy to rosyth. My shifts used to start at 6 pm and finished at 2 am. It was difficult for me to arrange pick ups at that time.

summary: Worth it if your manager is good
advice: If they don't already realise that they need to invest more in training new staff rather than churning bodies in and out the doors then nothing I tell them will change their minds.
pros:
There are still some really supportive and encouraging managers around.
There are worse places to go if you need some stable cash and aren't sure what you want to do.
cons:
Culture of short term solutions to long term problems.
Seems to be a continual trend in reducing initial training period and support, and yet management seem puzzled by why many new staff perform poorly.

advice: Consider that diversity means more than just the obvious!! ie consider colleagues who don't necessarily have a degree; there is still more you can do for females.  The majority of our customers don't have privaleged backgrounds / degrees.
pros: Prestigeous company with the usual perks of a large corporate.
cons: Officially career progression opportunity is there for all however far too many areas in the business with a "jobs for the boys" culture. In addition, due to relentless cost cutting, the only way to get on is coming through the grad scheme where these colleagues are prioritised for promotion opportunities.

advice: Continue the genuine focus upon people. Invest in your systems.
pros: Genuinely people focused organisation. Whilst not relevant to me, I saw more genuine focus and open discussion about mental health and work life balance than I had seen at any large organisation. Significant number of people - including those in the call centres - working their 5 day week over 4 days. Big employee satisfier and retention tool.
cons: Archaic systems. LBG is made up of many different banks that have been subsumed. As a result, there are inefficient processes and the pace of change can be improved quite slow.

summary: High Standards and a Great Journey.
advice:
-Continue to place Customers first. 
-Focus on what employees deliver, not what they look like? Practice meritocracy and not my mummy and daddy own this and that? 
- recognize REAL employees working in the background making things happen, putting in the hours, not showboats. 
-Cost Cutting on staff and cost-cutting on budgets to improve technology is not always the way and ultimately can hurt the customer.
- Weed out non-performing Senior Management, and especially those that try to use their position over others unfavorably.
- Embrace New CEO CNunn who certainly looks like a great fit in terms of Lloyds Values and Behaviours.

Overall still a great place to work.
pros:
- Some really good people that I had the pleasure of working with, both knowledgeable and clever. (my career spans +20 years in the city), 
- Lots of opportunities to get involved and make a real difference, both work-wise and the charities Lloyds supports.
- Fair transparent pay scales (for most) and remuneration package.
- Honest conversations to assist career and talent development, but some line managers were better at this than others.
- Motivational leadership from the top, although at times there were one or two egos (rotten eggs) out for their own cause.
-Diverse and inclusive (D&I) was/is prioritised.
-Staff Surveys/Polls/Staff workshops, Some Senior Management listened to staff and try to make improvements, others out for their own.
- Work-Life balance (for most) - although, I did hefty hours quite a lot, at times I did get recognised for the quality of my work and output, at other times I saw others steal my glory.
cons:
-Early years were tough (2010 - 2013) due to long hours, sorting out ledger systems flows and reporting as well as having to put up with some bad eggs spreading awful comments about other staff members and causing friction, one clicky group (all members from different teams) used to go for walks, pep talks, and ego massages on how to antagonise others. Head of that mob is still there. But, most people just wanted to get stuck in, do a good job and help out.
- Lot's of the good staff in London are gone due to re-orgs (cost-cutting) to Edinburgh and Bristol, but there is also a lot of good staff in London still there. A lot of the roles moved up to Edinburgh, so people in London left. The staff in Edinburgh are also very friendly.  It was a difficult time for many people in London, but people do need to grasp change. 
- Some staff free-riding (lazy) off the back of other staff's hard work, and prevent them from getting promoted, as if they did get promoted who would do the work. Hence, the Scorecard/Year-end review system was not always fair (Rating and Promotion favoritism), especially in the early years. 
-And it was widely known in the Year End collaboration meetings, Senior Managers would make ridiculous untrue comments to prevent more junior staff from getting a higher rating in their appraisal, often with no supporting evidence. Numerous individuals were caught out (names not given here). Hence, some very interesting promotions?  (my ratings were decent, but generally felt it was a flawed system).

summary: Transitioning to a new way of working
advice:
Keep supporting colleagues through difficult times
With Your Best, ensure management don't revert to calibration and scoring because it will only become the old way of doing performance development again
pros:
Great benefits (holidays, pension contributions, Flex package, car allowance)
Forward thinking and in the process of adopting Agile methodologies
Huge company means many opportunities
Strong on Diversity & Inclusion and Mental Health issues
Strong on Helping Britain Propser including supportign charities/fundraising/fund matching
cons:
Due to adopting new ways of working (Agile) the company is very much in transition and hasn't yet fully settled
Query whether the right people have been put into the right Transformation roles

pros: Good training course that teaches you a lot about general banking that you otherwise wouldn't know. The regular customers become the best part of the job. I was hired part-time but the hours were always there to essentially be full-time.
cons: Management is poor, the job is very repetitive sat at a cashier desk all day doing the same transactions. Longer serving staff were given set shifts, whereas new staff worked on a rota which was constantly changing so it was hard to plan life around this. All your holidays had to be booked at the start of the year, with new staff having last pick so an extremely unfair hierarchy.

advice: Look to offer more flexible and tangible salary expectations, and also look to create a better more integrated team
pros: A very well rounded company that offers excellent learning to progress, with (in some areas) a clear ability to speak one's mind and challenge idea's that were put out there. Bonuses and additional benefits were good (especially the share plans offered).
cons: Salary was not the best in the financial world, with most other banks offering close to 50% higher starting salaries. If looking to work in a multi site manner it's very difficult to achieve true transparency and create a team bond.

summary: Great, as long as you're not agency!
advice: Stop using agency workers as expendable beings, when making people managers, stop promoting women simply because you want to be seen as progressive, promote the best candidate, regardless of gender.
pros:
Good pay, Call swings, Customers respect you, General feel is quite good!
Overall the job is fantastic and once you learn the ropes, very easy.  Staff Mortgage tracking the BOE baserate.
cons: If you're a member of permanent staff it's fantastic, if you're agency, you're expendable at any time while on the hook with false promises of permanency. I suppose the older style systems for booking appointments could be more intuitive as well.

summary: LBG.... Not Great but Not Bad...
advice: Still to much red tape.. everything takes to long (from getting budget to getting resources to getting architecture approvals)
pros: People are good.. Projects are varied..
cons:
in Lloyds all the resources are charged out to various projects.. the problem is that often projects ask resources to do work without allocating time which means you end up doing work but have no code to charge it to --> which in turn means problems for you and your line management.

another issue in lloyds is that in order to get things done, it is very much a culture of who you know rather than going through the normal lines.

advice: Management are very good and accessible. On my floor during the internship, the MD took the time to get to know everyone, including myself.
pros:
Great working culture
Great work/life balance
Surprising number of really good opportunities. It is a very large company. 
The grad scheme is very well rounded, giving you four very good rotations throughout the bank.
cons:
The work/life balance comes at a trade-off of lower pay than you will receive elsewhere. This is not to say the pay is bad, it is just not in the top, top bracket. 
Your bonus will not be as big as in other banks

advice: Ensure management apply HR and appraisal policies equally, be more open minded about promoting from within, be more transparent about appraisal measures and giving effective feedback.
pros: Collaborative culture, friendly and open, good benefits package, good work/life balance, Breakthrough initiatives to support women and minorities into senior positions, signs of developing more flexible working patterns and challenging inefficient and outdated working practices.
cons: Inconsistent attitude to flexible working and sabbatical requests, approval depended entirely on the attitude of your own manager/senior manager and were not consistently applied, very difficult to progress internally from back to front office as progression was encouraged only to certain roles (usually within the same area).

advice: Value your people more. Senior management would get more out of their staff in tricky situations if they yelled less on conference calls and focused on coming up with viable solutions rather than apportioning blame and empire building / politics.
pros: Great company to work for. Easy going, friendly people (for the most part) and good wages.
cons: IT aspects of project management difficult to manage because lots of IT elements have been outsourced to 3rd parties who only have a limited service contact eg support is 9-5 5 days a week when project implementations are usually overnight and at weekends.

summary: Worst company i have ever worked for
advice: You need a complete overhaul of communication, processes and attitudes. Value your staff and create a better working environment.
pros: Good discounts on cinema tickets and other stuff on their internal site can get around 50% off cineworld
cons: Terrible atmosphere, customer facing colleagues always last to know important changes, drains the life out of you so any time an internal opportunity comes up there are plenty of people including management that will do anything to stop you succeeding. Little to no recognition for the hard work you put in. It is expected of you to put in unpaid hours in branch. In the branch network it is pre determined who will fill each vacancy and they essentially swap staff to fill vacancies - this is decided by managers not on merit but on who they choose.

advice: Management is great. Could sacrifice some time to help other develop and put more time into helping people understand.
pros: Amazing career opportunity which is flexible in many aspects which allows freedom to many individuals that need it. Working for Lloyds is a reward in it self and allows you to develop yourself into whatever you want to be.
cons:
It’s hard to fly up the ladder. I am 18 and I want to be the best I can’t be before I’m 21 this means I don’t have time to waste this is forcing me to leave and find something
That will help me achieve my goals of success.

pros: Share scheme was a nice bonus
cons: Toxic blame culture. Competition between peers encourage rather than collaboration

advice: Look at the people that have the skills and talent and let them guide you on what needs to be done rather than the people who are spending time inflating your ego vying for your attention.
pros: Don't work there unless there's a specific reason you have to. Benefits are good. Work-life balance is good depending on the manager you're working under.
cons: Colleagues in the design space are often trying to showcase themselves rather than doing the work. Juniors with 2 years of 'exposure' to design related skills are placed in senior/leadership positions and don't know what they are doing. It's about who you know not what you know or what you can deliver. Leadership are too busy fighting for titles and lime-light to prove themselves to actually help the people doing the job. You have to justify yourself. Projects get put on a 'shelf' so often you may as well not put in effort. It's either work ridiculous hours to achieve targets or you're bored because a business area has run out of budget and . You're often brought in at the tail end of a project rather than upfront where you'd provide more value, so you're often seen as a blocker to delivery (which drives bonuses) than a help. You have to justify and explain what you are there to do every time you change projects.

advice: stop training and having meetings for the sake of it,provide some real training  recognised by other employers. treat your front line staff with dignity and respect instead of complaining about there absence and performance.Promote people based on merit not because they are your pal or are good at chatting about the football/flirting.
pros: fairly relaxed call centre,people are great and promotion prospects are there if you get "In" with the right people..Greast benefits with the staff mortgage and financial products although this can be a debt spiral if you take everything they throw at you.
cons: very much a case of 'who you know to get a promotion' ,training below standard and largely justifying someones role  meetings for the sake of it, new upper management all the time, changing things then they leave and then the new head of centre tries to change things again so they can impress there own manager., lots of  staff been there for a long time with no intention to move on and therefore limiting the promotional prospects of others, Redundancy and job profileing is the norm and more to come due to the retai and customer facing side of the business dying out.

pros: Nice team to work with
cons: Stressful management. Not organised. Industry isnt going anywhere

advice: Theres a lot of dead wood at Lloyds, management believe the bad wood will leave by its own accord over time but its the good people leaving out of frustration and bad people staying because its an easy job with very low pressure and expectations. A lot of people who get promoted don't really have the experience or knowledge to support the role.
pros: Low pressure, good work life balance, there are some long terms chances for promotion, reasonable salary. Long term picture for company looks good in present economic environment.
cons: Heavy politics with lots of people vying for attention, incredibly slow projects and general work (can be 4x longer to complete a task than competitors), while there are some things to learn its v slow to learn new things, poor quality team mates with low experience, no real direction or management from directors, technology is v poor (takes 30 odd mins to get into your laptop). Generally bad culture - overly politically correct. A lot of people leave due to boredom or not being recognised. Bonus is paid in shares and not cash.

summary: Huge problems and lack of management, poor training and support for new employee
advice: Managers should be good organisers and leaders not only salesman. Customer first, isn't it? Follow one best way. Back office person minimum 1 per branch, phone calls to the call centre not to the cashier. Take more care about the cashiers they are the face of the company!
pros:
Friendly colleagues.
Helpful HR
Nice/good uniform (for man)
1 hour lunch break.
Colleague offers.(pension and flex)
cons:
Morning meetings - always about targets nothing about team work or thx for the good job or plans
Training - nothing about the actual job.
Sometimes shortage of forms, stationary and most importantly short of staff. 
Promised but unpaid Overtime - usually 3 days from 5
Useless computer keyboard/touch-pad (IT really slow and useless, really effect your job in front of the customers)
Lots of paper waste (lots of unused prints from the fax and printers be shredded)
Software not user friendly.
If u made a mistake no way to find out what happened.
Different instructions from each manager.
Low basic salary. 
Reaching your targets is really depend on which branch are you in and where.
Customers fed up from up-sales. 
Running pick up the phone.(every 5 min)
Organised, sometimes dusty, dirty workplace.

advice:
Cut out the dead wood and invest in young talent.
Invest in IT.
pros:
Work-life balance on the whole is good.
People generally quite nice with a relaxed culture.
Supportive working environment, even if the awful IT doesn't help at times.
If you like an easy life, or somewhere to go to retire (as a fair few seem to do) it's the place for you.
cons:
I.T. is awful.
Full of very average people and a lot of people who think they're a lot better than they actually are, often trying to build their little empires.
Lots of 'lifers' who block progress of younger talent, massive bottleneck at middle grades.
External hires paid significantly more for the same role.
Talent is clearly not recognised with promotion often going to those who lack ability but do the face time. Staff often rated unfairly as management have quotas to apply to ratings.
Many top heavy teams and there's more focus on 'performance management' and presenting meaningless stats to management in powerpoint format so they can justify their salary. Those at lower grades are over-worked.
Risk-adverse culture now means the group is often behind the curve and playing catch up in the market.

summary: A good experience overall, however it really is dependent on which branch you work at.
pros: For a customer assistant, it is the best paid role compared to other competitors. I believe there are many benefits to the role, such as work/life balance is very good. The people I worked with are amazing, and it was the first time I experienced working in a close-knit team. The result of this was, if you were behind on sale targets, your colleagues could give you some of theres if they have performed better than expected. Good performance is definitely recognised, and merited for.
cons: A lot of pressure is put on selling ANYTHING, even if you are misselling. Could effect your work experience and environment. I found, depending on your branch and manager, promotional opportunities are very hard to come by. This is quite disheartening for an individual who has a focused career path and motivations, but their manager is stopping them from progressing. I feel the work culture is very much stuck in the past and hasn't moved on with the times, and the likelihood of progressing is dependent on how chummy you are with the superiors/management.

advice: Stop trying to find ways to target people and put pressure on to sell products customers haven't come in for.
pros: Targets are slowly being banned, the FCA stop them from targeting you on one thing, the bank thinks of another way to target/pressure you then 6 months later the FCA will ban them from that too, They'll then try another way and so on and so on.
cons:
Very sales orientated, don't be fooled by the "helping customers" speak, you are there to sell loans, credit cards, home insurance etc and if you aren't doing those you aren't doing your job.
Very micro managed, you have to have a meeting with your line manager ( who 9/10 has never done the job and couldn't sell anything to anyone ) at the start of the day, you have to mid brief every customer meeting you have, appointment or quick walk in, and then a meeting at the end of the day to explain and review everything you have done, or in most cases what you haven't done. 18 years experience and still treated like a child.

advice: Have the courage and conviction to develop a five year business plan for the wholesale bank, communicate it and stick with it.
pros: Lloyds has somehow managed to maintain an old school British banking culture where there is a real emphasis on supporting each other and collaborating. People coming in from other banks often remark on this. This makes it a great place to get some training as a graduate and an more pleasant environment for people seeking to get out of aggressive institutions.
cons: Currently the wholesale bank is shrinking as the group deleverages and the bank is increasingly risk adverse. There is clearly going to be a reduction in headcount and the opportunities to advance are extremely limited. There is also uncertaintly about the future of many business units. Many people internally critisise the management team for being to risk adverse and so giving up opportunities to make money, however the business model going forwards clearly is to be a low risk/ stable returns bank - if that is not what you are looking for then it is not likely to be the place for you.

summary: Terrible culture of blame and bullying in main IT areas, and is hugely bureaucratic and immobile.
advice: Accept that it's not working, and change tack. And it's no good paying lip service to people culture. You actually HAVE to walk the walk as well as talk the talk.
pros: Decent amount of holiday. Reasonable benefits. UK-based staff in junior roles work well as a team.
cons: Benefits eroded by stealth in recent years. Failure of management to accept that the many issues in the past few years are due to policy of offshoring key roles. Other key people have been overwhelmed and left before the workload made them ill. Bullying, finger pointing, penny pinching, and an incredible amount of red-tape have made it essentially impossible to do anything to a good standard.

summary: Pay gaps, lack of support for mental health issues, over the top management
advice:
Stop micromanaging staff, leave them to their own devices and you’ll probably get better results 
Have better systems in place for employees who have mental health issues 
Look at the pay gaps for staff who do the same role 
Get rid of old school bullying managers
pros:
Good benefits package 
Flexible working hours if needed 
Could usually always get holidays days I asked for 
Training is pretty good 
Some lovely people who don’t believe that Lloyds js the best thing since sliced bread (they have a life outside of work)
cons:
THE MOST RIDICULOUS PAY GAPS!!!! Myself earning 18k someone doing the SAME ROLE as me with not much more experience on 30k plus!!!! All due to the bank having a switch around with role definitions. 

Management get really upset with any kind of criticism all they do if defend banks policies without hearing from frontline colleagues, then when it doesn’t work they suddenly agree....always felt like I wasn’t listened to. 

Awful attitudes/procedures in dealing with mental health issues and taking time off due to this (no help from HR either) was made to feel like I was a hassle to deal with.

Some managers are really stuck in old sales and performance attitudes, putting pressure on staff 
Job roles keep changing, adding more and more to the role without pay  

A lot of micromanagement
Always changing the way the day is structured, trying to come up with ways to make it look like the bank isn’t ‘selling’ to customers when in reality targets still matter
Upper management, local directors etc are far too fake and you can tell they only want progression 
Not allowed to have an opinion that differs from the banks position- will be put on a ‘report’ to ‘manage behaviour’

summary: Safe company, but lacking strategic direction.
advice: Every colleague should be able to tell you what the strategy of the Group is - at the moment they can't do this. Talent is lost due to the highly bureaucratic processes of Lloyds which the executives don't even see, as there are just too many layers.
pros: Good benefits, good work life balance, very flexible

summary: Good company but they ask for too much from staff
advice: I think Lloyds is a good company overall, and it means well. In the big picture, it obviously does many things right and I do believe that more senior executives can be trusted. But lower managerial level is different and my main advice would to absolutely treat colleagues with respect and basically don't bully because there is no gain from that. Secondly, there should be change around sickness and absence and trusting colleagues more. Thirdly, which is more specific to Business Banking, Business Managers should have much more control than they currently do, because most of the time Business Managers have to pass instructions to other departments to action requests, creating a higher risk of error - just give the Business Managers more control. Generally speaking though, management do a good job considering the resources they have under the pressures they have and implementing the ideas above would make Lloyds a nice, comfortable place to work.
pros: Pay is ok and the rewards and benefits are very good. It's nice to be part of a large well-established company with an internationally recognisable name. Generally, the people are nice and quite fun. Progression and side-steps are definitely possible if you make it happen. Lloyds do focus on the community and want to make a positive impact and are good at organising events. Training programmes for most job roles are truly excellent. Holiday requests and time off are normally quite easy to request and amend.
cons: There is still a big, clear focus on numbers, and tracking colleague's performance on 'how much' rather than 'how well' somebody has done - more so than other banks I have worked in. Especially in a contact centre, everything you do is timed and recorded. Corporate bullying exists, especially with absence and sickness - there is only a small time period in the morning you may call in sick and colleagues have expressed anxiety in calling in sick. I've only been sick one day during my time and Lloyds were not supportive or helpful in the process. As with a lot of workplaces, there are good and bad managers, but it is not uncommon for me to witness (almost daily) managers shouting at other colleagues, attacking them personally, to make them feel worthless - which is extremely unprofessional and a form of bullying. There is no time or room for colleague interaction - I could go through most of my day working in a room of 40 people but not speak to any of them due to the workload intensity. There are many conflicting procedures which cause delays in customer resolutions. Also there is a blame culture and a big problem with issues being 'passed on'.
