summary: Alright at first, destroys your soul eventually.
advice: Update your systems. Hire better managers. Get rid of the exception system - allow people some leeway for bathroom and screen breaks (seriously the 2% ADH leeway you have just now doesn't cut it for 10 hour shifts). Have a better progression system (Give people an eventual route off the phone). Don't get people to open a current account with you to get their salary paid into - what kind of company does this? Forcing your (average) products on people? Come on.
pros:
Job security. If this is your thing - stay as long as you want.

Sick pay. Best thing about the job. After the initial first year or so people start taking loads of sick leave because the job sucks so much. Seriously: Why is everyone depressed, Lloyds?

Good holidays and holiday booking system.

Reputable company to have on the CV if you want your foot in the door of banking.
cons:
First up - and this isn't much to do with Lloyds itself, it's call centre work. It's nothing more, it's nothing that takes any degree of intelligence or depth as a person, they literally hire anyone. Seriously - they hire ANYONE to take these calls. All you're doing for the most part is transferring money for people, telling them their balance, typing their complaints, listening to them moan about you and the bank. If you're lucky they'll promote you and get you to read scripts all day downgrading bank accounts and applying for overdrafts (lending is system driven - you'd just be reading the script). If you don't mind call centres - this might be one of the better ones from what I've heard, but I can't speak to that from experience. 

Your time at Lloyds in Customer Contact will depend on your manager and their management style. I went through about 5 or 6 different managers in my time here, a couple (the ones that left you alone) made me think the place wasn't so bad. The rest of them are all jobsworth drones devoid of any and all life or personality. I won't name names but seriously some of the managers at Lloyds should NOT be managing people. They're like actual robots. 

Archaic systems. Seriously one of the systems (EDGE) hasn't been updated since the early 1990's. The other systems (PBS, Desktop) are at least 15-20 years old. They break all the time. How can a bank this wealthy have systems from a different era? 

Exceptions. Do you have to go to the bathroom? Better write a detailed note explaing exactly what you did at the bathroom and why, and send it to your manager via email at the end of the day. They'll then probably have a meeting with you asking why you need to use the bathroom during shift. Disciplinary if you keep needing the toilet, slave!

Literally everyone hates their job. I don't know anyone who's passionate about what they do. It's just braindead work, somewhere to collect a pay cheque and count down until retirement or death. 

I never intended on staying as long as I did. It was alright for the first year, but then it got worse and worse, and you hate it more and more. My advice is this: If you're thinking of only working here short term - stick to that plan. Don't stay too long - you'll get PTSD.

No progression in customer contact. Do you want to move from the phones to a back office/analyst role? Better look outside of Lloyds.

Nonsense values. This company has no morals. They're a massive & cold banking institutiun. Their purpose is to make money for the shareholders and that's IT. Don't let them tell you otherwise.

Also, you don't have to open a Lloyds account to get your salary paid into. They were paying my salary into an external account for years just fine. This is just a way of getting more customers - it's totally unethical.

summary: Great organisation for personal development, not so good for career progression
advice: Try to understand skills and expertise of your direct reports before making them redundant
pros:
Excellent support environment and ample opportunities for pesonal development. Company is moving towards developing colleague engagement and strong focus on diversity inclusion as well as providing great opportunities for personal development. 
Good range of flexible benefits
Several internal opportunities and great environment to work with
cons:
Lower payscales - mainly for permanent and heritage staff memebers
Higher frequency of structural changes leading to lack of understanding between management and staff
Numerous projects with poor management
Poor standards of training for admin staff and a lot of focus on cost cutting

advice: Resign and go to pension. Way to young minds! Too big exposure to retail mortgages. Wait for the next property crush!
pros: Ability to work from home
cons: Managers get assigned to positions based on politics. My manager was arrogant, absolutely clueless and lacked any understanding of how to manage people and about business area. This is unbelievable because his salary is huge. Not interesting boring job, not smart colleagues. Nothing to learn. Terrible amount of time spent on performance management, ratings are given based not on real performance but politics. This is unacceptable. Bad management by not appropriate people. Low salary with very long career progression. Worst working place ever. Discriminative culture covered by diversity and inclusion which actually doesn't exist. If you come from different culture, they will not accept you and make you suffer.

pros:
Being the only intern I was given a lot of exposure to clients and senior members of the bank. Work will not always land on your desk; to make the most of the 10 weeks you have to be proactive. This could mean going round members of staff asking for work or coming up with your own projects based on initiative and onervations.
The senior management team were great and very supportive.
cons: With every job comes the tedious admin work. However, this only took up a small part of my time at the bank (an amount that was representative to a permanent role).

summary: Don't expect any career progression - jobs for the boys
advice: Stand by your cultural pledges and recognise colleagues from all walks have life have something to offer and are worthy of promotion.
pros:
Good perks of a large corporate
Good image with peers which should look good on your cv
Culture is good re diversity, work life balance although not always filtered through to all areas
cons:
Don't expect your career progress to be quick - unless you are in with the right management.  If you haven't got a degree forget it altogether
Pay progression very very slow
Continual programme of restructuring and head count reduction mean some areas of the group completely ineffective

summary: Seems like a typical slightly old-fashioned, stuffy corporate environment
advice: Remove some layers, change the culture from one where senior people only seem to talk to their superiors and "direct reports" (an ugly phrase), and give people the opportunity to prove themselves and progress
pros: Good work/life balance (for most people at least), generous support for professional qualifications.  Very positive aspirations, currently successful and on an upward trajectory.  The "nice" bank which actually purports to genuinely care about its customers, and also currently the most profitable bank in the UK.
cons: Poor or inexistent in-house training, excessively hierarchical atmosphere, highly bureaucratic and process-driven approach, opaque performance management and career progression

advice: i think that they try to get it right everytime but the one thing that led to my exit was that i found getting promoted or moving departments was too political. a fair and transparent process would be awesome.
pros: There were so many things that i learnt at Lloyds that have helped me in future roles. met some amazing people and had a wonderful time working for a company that i feel really looks after its staff.
cons: could do with being more decisive when reacting to feedback either from staff or customers but not the end of the world.

pros:
Group Digital is an exciting and growth area of the organisation, with key capabilities being brought in to transform the organisation into a more flexible and customer focused business. 
An exciting and emerging digital culture is obvious in Group Digital, supported by significant financial and leadership support, which is permeating the thinking of the most senior leaders in the organisation. Colleagues and reward are good and the level of scale, reach and UK impact is attractive.
cons: There are still challenges, particularly in hardware to support productivity, however this has recently become a focus for management and is improving.

advice: Don't forget who your most loyal and hard working colleagues are. Value medium to long term employees as they think of the business as theirs and will go the extra mile to try to protect it. Be careful that the headlong push for Diversity is not done in a way that destroys the morale of elements of the work force. Notwithstanding the foregoing, be prepared to be radical in resizing the business to face up to the very real competitive challenges you are now facing. If you don't then the business may suffer terminally.
pros: You only appreciate the quality of an employer when you can look at it dispassionately from the outside in. Lloyds is a very well organised and run business. As an employee in a managerial or senior managerial role you generally have an interesting and demanding job working with good quality clients and other colleagues. The premises are in decent shape, there is a very good support network for It, Hr etc and above all else it is well paid with decent benefits albeit these are being chipped away at bit by bit most notably in terms of pensions of older colleagues.
cons: I perceive the Bank to be at a crossroads in its evolution as it is struggling to remain competitive in a market where new challenger banks as well as traditional players are vying for the most lucrative tranches of the market. The business may need to slim down a lot more and become more agile to be able to compete. The Bank is also obsessed with Diversity and forcing through changes to the workforce to produce stats to impress whoever is interested. For me the Bank should be focussing upon getting the best workforce it can and if that meant that say 70% of senior colleagues were of Chinese or Asian origin on merit then so be it. Most middle aged white heterosexual male employees feel that they are being discriminated against and no-one bats an eyelid.

summary: Jack of all trades, master of none.
advice:
Treat your staff like people rather than machines ESPECIALLY during this difficult time. Colleagues that face customers (which are not selling products, but rather maintaining the services surrounding them) need more acknowledgement, the bottom grade of colleagues get so much work dumped on them and they do not have a voice. Sales get treated better because they bring money into the business, but due to the COVID-19 lockdown; Sales were actually CLOSED while Servicing remained open with no change in opening times, dealing with the overflow of anxiousness and fright from customers. A few of my colleagues have messaged me personally saying how tired they are, how upset they have become and how their voices are not heard.

I love working for Lloyd’s as my manager in particular is very supportive and my whole team (including staff from other teams) are very close, we always speak to each other asking for help if other managers are unavailable to support us. 

Promises get made to lighten our workload, only for it to happen a year later and get it dumped back on us after a few weeks. We all need to be apart of the same team and not treat colleagues differently based on their grade. We’ve all worked hard - before, during and after COVID-19 (we all hope it will hopefully settle).

I believe that certain matters need to be looked into, and colleagues should be experience / overlook work in different areas so that they can understand what each area does and how important their role is.
pros:
Annual pay review.
Annual bonus - dependant on group and personal performance.
Free group shares.
A wide variety of colleagues from all different backgrounds.
Possible career progression.
cons:
You can take on many different brand types, if one brand is more popular than the others, they get forgotten about and it makes it difficult to remember knowledge of other brands.
Older / longer serving staff are treated better in regards to flexible shifts and having to choice to not take on extra brand knowledge.
Some (not all) of the managers don’t even know the information about the brand that the company is forcing you to learn. You feel like you’re on your own and not getting much support.
Especially during the pandemic, the customers and queries can be VERY repetitive, it can make you feel upset, tired and frustrated, while they expect you not to have emotions during this time.
If you have knowledge on a specific brand and there aren’t many colleagues that are trained on the same brand, it becomes really difficult to arrange progression from your current role, but others that declined to be trained on that brand get better opportunities due to a lower risk of losing valuable colleagues.

advice:
More face to face interaction with homeworkers.
Having almost everything available online is detrimental to mental health.
You need human interaction
pros:
If your looking for stability & long term, fantastic pension of you max out your 6% contribution, share match program has increased significantly & now that shift patterns have been updated to work for you, convenient.
Really lovely colleagues that are genuine.
Managers that try there best.
cons:
It’s time to get back to the office after homeworking for over a year.
For mental health purposes at the minimum it would be nice to go in at least once a week.

advice: Don't micro -manage and listen to colleague suggestions more. Lloyd's is supposed to be a relationship bank, it isn't market competitive in its products - is supposedly all customer orientated, so let staff provide good service to customers by listening to what they want and tailoring that service to meet their needs. The low level staff are the ones dealing with customers/regulars day in day out, trust them. Data doesn't tell the whole picture.
pros:
Good benefits
Nice colleagues
Clear progression routes
Nice shade of green for the uniform
cons:
Constant abuse from customers
Pay not indicative of stress from customers
Bad management in places
Nepotism

summary: It was great at the start...
advice:
Treat your staff as people, not numbers
Extend the training period - more call listening and SUPPORTED stints on the phone
Add more support staff for your newbies
BE THERE DURING TRAINING - Our manager almost never was and this was apparently not uncommon. It made for quite a culture shock when we hit the real shifts.
pros:
Better workplace culture than most - Really kept us on the hook

Decent pay and benefits

"Hire by attitude" policy (apparently)- didn't serve well for retaining staff but the people I worked with were generally lovely

The shift pattern made for a good work-life balance
cons:
We all felt rushed through training, and rapidly lost staff as soon as we left. It felt like a sinking boat, all of us wondering who was next to leave.
This was excused by telling us that we would "learn better on the job", but due to the nature of the business there was very little margin for error and we felt woefully unprepared.

The few support staff we had regularly rolled their eyes at us for asking questions about calls regarding things that we had NEVER EVEN EXPECTED because we were told in training they almost never happened and we wouldn't need to know- they ended up occurring at least 3 times daily.
Then , despite a claimed "no statistics" culture (that was praised to no end during training) management would pull you on high hold times - at least two thirds of which was waiting for support to tell us what on earth was happening!

Very little support and the managers seemed more concerned with their own stats than their staff - Heard our manager more than once encouraging trainers to push us harder so that we would "pass" on time, and then telling us to our faces that we were doing fine and the training was supposed to ramp up like this.

Seeing that the building was almost perpetually empty should have been the first red flag.

summary: If you enjoy applying for your own job several times a year with the threat if redundancy, LBG could be for you.
advice: You can only treat your staff so badly for so long without suffering the consequences of a highly demotivated workforce. PS You have particular issues in Scottish Widows.
pros: Benefits package is reasonable though it has gradually been eroded over time.
cons: Traditional Banks are slow to change and stuck in the past - this is very clear at Lloyds where cost cutting is king. The bank likes to reduce headcount costs by creating an environment of perpetual uncertainty - only the strongest (or most desperate) hang around. This is not a company to plan a career in - you are simply a number - a dispensable one

summary: Paralysed by lack of decision making.
pros: Very flexible employer, enables people to work from home or other locations as and when they want
cons:
Three big issues:
- continual cuts to almost all areas means solutions to customer problems end up half baked at the 11th hour to save money.
- ALL change is difficult - getting decisions can be very difficult and decisions are often undone further down the line which becomes frustrating.
- There is now so much admin it has become a large part of any job, this is because of cuts to support staff as part of ‘efficiency savings’.

pros:
People
Reward Package
Flexibility for home work life balance before they decided to try and bring everyone back into the office.
cons:
High management trying to make a name for themselves without understanding the needs and complexities of the business area and their ability to do the work proficiently whether or not they were in the office or working from home. 
Area I worked for moved from a very flexible work life balance, working from home, to a situation where I would have to travel to either 1 of 2 locations outside of my acceptable commute.

summary: Great opportunities ahead if you are proactive.
advice: It'd be so much better if development would be more emphasised and if employees were given more lee way to work independantly.
pros: The company offers lots of opportunities for training, development and career progression. Most senior management is very open to suggestions and learning; mentoring and job shadowing are encouraged.
cons: The pay is not really top of the range and there is quite a bit of bureaucracy and politics. If you want a promotion you really have to invest time into getting there as it's not the most transparent workplace.

advice: Focus on the groups values and how you can bring these to life using tangible examples, interview format is linked in heavily with these. Remember to use STAR
pros: Lloyds has great colleague offers that are very comprehensive. The absences policy is very supporting for those that need it and the company has lots of opportunities for those willing to develop.
cons: You can often feel like a number and have little imput from projects that impact you. Systems and processes change almost daily and it can often be difficult to keep up with the change.

advice: Stop promoting people just because they asked for it ... also look at promoting part time staff who have years of experience and would make great mama gets. It would just take a bit of planning from yourselves to organise more job share opportunities... they're non existent at the moment and you're missing out on a wealth of skills and knowledge.
pros: Really help with flexible hours, they never turned me down in requests for changing working hours as my son grew up, but I was careful to be reasonable in my requests.
cons: They often promote people into management positions because they've asked for it. This results in some inexperienced people trying to run depts and branches with no clue what they're doing. I saw some really immature outbursts from young managers, actual physical temper tantrums sometimes.

summary: Great culture but a lot of red tape
advice: Update software to match the other uk banks! it's a must.
pros: Brilliant working culture and people, despite just being an intern I really felt welcomed.  Focus on serving the client and training is available if needed.
cons: The salary's are lower that that of most other competing banks but about 5--10k. There is a lot of red tape and some of the processes within the department I worked could be sped up. The software is very outdated and causes issue for many clients and staff.

summary: Used to be a fantastic place to work
advice: Try and get to a point of steadiness within the organisation, the size of cuts and the constant change within the organisation has created a climate of fear and doesn't produce an environment where people feel valued.
pros:
- Good salary and benefits, very well paid compared to other sectors.
- Excellent work/life balance.
- Staff are generally great to work with.
cons:
- Too much uncertainty year on year.
- Strange decisions seem to be made by Senior Management.
- Not enough time between restructuring to allow sufficient time to assess the effectiveness of change.

advice: Listen to staff, develop real training, reward loyal colleagues rather than the ones who want to leave.
pros: Friendly colleagues, central locations, occasional work from home, nice holiday package with the opportunity to buy/sell more. Inclusive culture.
cons: Too many meetings for the sake of it, more project management and change people than those actually doing the job. Endless E-learning packages rather than real training, too slow to change and senior management disconnected from staff. Limited opportunities to progress unless you threaten to leave. Pay not in line with competitors.

summary: This is the best job I have worked at, my team are more like a family to me.
advice: Most of the time, you guys are great, some of the times, you let work stresses, deadlines etc bring you down which you then in turn inflict on your colleagues with your bad mood! Try not to let your mood affect how you behave with your colleagues.
pros: Imagine spending the entire day with good friends, laughing, getting along, enjoying your time - that's how it feels like at my work place, it makes me more productive with work and work doesn't feel like a chore. It's fun.
cons: The main challenge I find is progression. I achieve good ratings every year, I am highly respected among my peers and managers but there just aren't enough opportunities to progress to the next level up.

summary: Lloyds is a great place to work, if you are happy staying exactly where you are
advice: Consider that if you continue to suppress the progression of your more ambitious colleagues, they may lose morale, feeling that their efforts are going unrewarded. This may mean that you eventually lose them entirely to another division or even another company, just so that you can keep your number of each role type consistently diverse.
pros: They are very focused on the colleague experience, and on development within your role.
cons: If you are an ambitious person, they can sometimes make it difficult to progress further up the career ladder - they can seem more concerned with maintaining the correct statistics within the Division, than harnessing your personal potential to give you new challenges.

advice: Listen to your workforce!
pros:
It looks good on your CV?

Some good staff discounts also
cons:
The management are hit and miss. Some of the management have been promoted just because they have been there since BC not because they are actually decent at what they do.

Wage is horrific! Can get more in a call centre. 

Move you around branches without hardly any notice or thought for the colleagues circumstances.

You will only get promoted if your face fits. Promotions are NOT based on merit. It is clear to see when you meet some of the assistant branch managers and branch managers.

Only get paid from 9am - 5pm when you have to be in at 8:45am in the morning and don't leave until 6-6:30pm some evenings.

advice: Great place to grow your career as development is really important to Lloyds and they do care about people. So if you want to develop and grow your career I'd recommend as an employer
pros: The company is people and customer focused with the aim of putting both at the heart of decisions. Joining such a large corporate really does open up many opportunities for you and development is high on the agenda to identify talent internally and progress within.
cons: Reputation has been tarnished following the acquisition of HBOS and the thousands of job losses that happened due to integrating the two businesses which can still cause unease. A big focus is cost control and stripping out waste which again can cause unease however the aim is to do it in the right way for customers, people and shareholders.

summary: The best experience you can get
advice: Listen! Build a strong team around you and you will fair well
pros: Learning a marketing trade from the best in the business. Standards and expectations are incredibly high but you will develop skills that other employees will really value
cons: Overly complex and time consuming sign off procedures that were introduced in later years meant you always  felt you were trying to do your job with both hands tied behind your back. I am sure that now the company is back to strength these have been relaxed.

advice: The diversity and inclusion campaign is working well and so is the encouragement of participation in charities. Rest mentioned above.
pros: It is one of the biggest Financial Services companies in the UK with a presence in retail and commercial banking, insurance, PWM etc and should therefore have ample career opportunities. This does exist to some extent. Second the Director level management has the right mindset to encourage employees but is somewhat ruined by middle level managers who only see things for their profit/short term gain. Many charities to participate in and the company cares about diversity
cons: Repeated department changes creates a sense of insecurity and can demoralise staff, Mid level managers need to be taken to task for their selfish pursuits and not supporting sub-ordinates enough but claiming to their bosses they do

summary: Overall a great place to work
advice: For the senior leadership team - stop hiring “yes people” for middle management. Instead hire those who have great ideas, balanced skills and a good amount of general intelligence.
pros:
- Inclusive environment 
- Supportive colleagues 
- Friendly people 
- Plenty of personal development opportunities
- Additional benefits such as medical insurance, share plans and a generous pension matching plan
- Pay is okay - with additional benefits it becomes a better package (much better than other UK banks)
cons:
Management can be very poor - especially middle management - and progression is based on who likes you and who is a “yes person” rather than your capabilities

Management (in some instances) will provide lip service rather than actual support 

Pay in other banks is better however the overall package at LBG is more attractive

advice: Be real and no shady business.
pros: Great salary and benefits. Company cares about well-being and helped me with time off when I was going through a personal turmoil. They offer great opportunities for development, lots of events and groups to join.
cons: It's a big corporation, so making any change takes ages and needs to be approved by too many people. Very risk adverse, which is understandable looking at the past experiences of the banking industry. I feel that my quirky personality is dumped and everyone should be the same serious worker.

advice: Take a look at the work the staff do before sending out e-mails, stating all is in order and going to plan, when it clearly is not.
pros: No probationary period, so feel free to do nothing and get away with murder. Take advantage of the minimal training expense available.
cons:
Bureaucratic, low pay, no promotion prospects, senior management who don't have the relevant experience or qualifications.

There are some senior managers / directors who are only school leavers or have non-relevant degrees such as psychology, yet are in charge of vital technical areas, such as quant and risk.

Salaries are capped, so if you are at the top of the payscale, you won't receive a raise. What incentive is there for you to work hard?

Bonuses are low and also capped (at 10%) and not paid until JUNE! Which other company does that?

The politics are a major problem. There are contractors running the show, in charge of permanent staff, when it should be the other way round.

advice:
Complete exit interviews to understand how you can change your business for the better.
Have one central site for policies and procedures instead of hive/random sharepoints for every team/project.
pros: Good pensions scheme, flexible working environment. Progressive employee health policy.
cons:
Basic salary and grading of roles is appalling - everyone working the grade above their role for less money.
Teams, work and divisions are very silo'd - lack of community and communication.
Line managers are good people leaders but often have no knowledge of the the roles they are managing.

summary: Recommend for banking servicing, great ethos surrounding providing a service to its clients.
advice: Spend more resources in to the professional development of staff.
pros:
Some great people in the offices, one of the better introductions in to banking servicing with a range of teams specialising across current accounts, savings, credit cards, mortgages, and my area being in fraud and disputes.
There are opportunities to work in both front line and back office to support BAU processes. Friendly working environment with open floor office spaces.
cons: Lack of support for further qualifications such as accounting or finance.

summary: Safe and reasonable if you're willing to put in the work
advice: Keep doing what you're doing but it will take a while to earn trust.  There is a lot of change fatigue - consider it non-critical changes could be phased to avoid disengagement, particularly organisational change.
pros: Reasonably secure despite market.  Pay has been upgraded recently at manager / associate director level.  Decent perks & holidays.  For a PM there is generally flexibility on working hours, location etc.
cons: Pay is still lower than some of the competition - be prepared for a consultant reporting to you on twice your salary (not contractor).   There are definite differences between the divisions & roles in terms of expectation and reward.  Flexibility is a strength but too much still depends on local managers expectations / bias.

advice:
Have longer term strategy with long term investment, rather than short term and pull funding before a project is complete
Needs to be better process for colleagues to get promoted rather than them having to apply for a role
pros:
Flexible working
Annual leave entitlement
Great people
Learning widely encouraged with time dedicated for your own learning
cons:
Sometimes can feel 'too big' with lots of legacy architecture
Some areas still feel quite siloed and there can be red tape due to it's size, complexity and risk appetite making it slow to change at times

pros: Can't think off one to be honest. It's a job if you're really stuck
cons: Basic pay and for what you're expected to do. Managers in Belfast did not have much knowledge on mental health so didn't treat everyone fairly. Micro managed to the bone it was a disgrace. One minute late back from toilet and expected to answer for that one minute. I went from a bubbly happy person into someone that refused to get out of bed in the mornings. You have to lick to progress anywhere so people that haven't been in business long were getting further than people that had been there longer that actually know the job. Two Saturdays a months and then they said we need to work three maybe 4 out of the month.

summary: Poorly managed in the IT department at a senior level - far too much politics and problem shifting.
advice:
- Be genuinely transparent about your plans and let the teams execute them
- Stop micro-managing
- Simplify operations
pros:
- Good work-life balance
- Salary is OK - not special but OK
- Overall bank leadership has the right strategy
- Good culture amongst lower levels to help get things done
cons:
- IT management is excessively short-term - constant firefighting at the expense of long-term plans
- Culture of problem-shifting - not solving problems
- No willingness to address difficult issues

advice: Be more visible.
pros:
Career progression is feasible - very much a meritocracy once you're in the door on a permanent contract. Easy to shift laterally before shifting up.
Very open to personal development, funding qualifications relevant to role or likely career direction.
Gradual erosion of the old guard / jobs for the boys. Work/life balance is good, as are benefits and salary.
cons:
Change is frustratingly slow, with decisions by committee. Accountability of project failings is low.
any spend needs to go through a bureaucratic and lengthy process designed to encourage apathy.

advice: Allow more innovative approaches to leadership and encourage entrepreneurial behaviour in less senior staff.
pros: Dependant upon your role there are numerous agile working options. Lloyds are big on community work and will allow you to use work time for volunteering. Self development is hugely encouraged.
cons: The company has a very much siloed structure and departments often operate as separate companies. Culture is very much dependant on the area that you work in, meaning that experiences can differ largely across the organisation. Progression and bonus measures can be very dependant on whether your manager likes you, more so than it is about merit and the quality of work. The bank is far too risk adverse and is not open to much innovation in most parts of the bank besides Group digital.

summary: Management need training in people skills, look at the stress they are causing people
advice: Sort your lower management teams out there are more people of sick with stress than I have ever known Managers lie about company policies like they really think you are not going to check absolutely ridiculous
pros: Good pay, benefits, people management excluded although there are a couple that are good
cons: More focused on stats and figures rather than the pressure and stress they are putting staff under totally under understaffed, but don’t give a damn they expect you to carry on and meet SLA’s when you are doing the work of 2-3 people “CARNAGE”

advice: The above may be changing but if it hasn't, I suggest treat genders equally with respect to pay and bonuses.
pros: flexible working, including working from home. good benefits.  Hot on documentation and processes. competitive rates of pay
cons:
disparity in pay between genders.  pay increases and bonuses for part time workers  poor despite quality of performance.  frequent restructure requiring employees to reapply for their jobs.
I should add I took voluntary redundancy in 2010. the drop down list above only went back as far as 2013 and I had to select something to submit review

summary: Progression barriers, pay progression very poor
advice: Try harder to retain talent by creating opportunities. Change your recruitment practices. Scrap competency questioning. Abandon performance ratings fitting to a curve. Create opportunities outside of London for all of the great regional talent.
pros: Stable environment on the whole, staff mortgage (base rate, capped at £200k), good perks (4% flex cash, £4kpa company car allowance, pension top up of 8% on employee putting in 3% rising to a 13% top up when employee puts in 5% can be very fast growing). Can be good internal training opportunities, will find budget for professional qualifications, will generally retain staff even during reshuffles. Is a good business with good prospects for the future and strong leadership. Culture is generally very good.... outside of London. Inside London it’s very poor, and sadly this is where there are most opportunities. Great talent and leadership outside London, but not many opportunities.
cons: Total barrier in progression to senior management. I’ve been in the business a decade and never known anyone to be promoted from manager / associate Director to senior manager / Director, which equates externally to a senior associate going to VP. This progression barrier is due to constant reshuffles, job cuts and compression at VP level. A huge number of staff waiting for a redundancy package at senior level. Majority of business unwilling to cut loose under performers looking for a payoff - on the other side the asset management team are far too aggressive and will toss you out like cattle with a toxic culture. A lot of weak senior management that gets shuffled from one team to the next. True talent gets well coached internally then leaves the business for progression, leaving behind a lot of weak players. Black hole of decision makers in GC and FI leading to a total absence of control. Associates in GC and FI are mostly preppy and entitled work dodgers, and the true talent sadly often doesn’t get the spotlight they deserve.

advice: Huge favoritism of certain colleagues at this site who are protected by  senior management.  This caused a lot of bad feeling and other more deserving colleagues were overlooked.
pros: Wonderful colleagues and outstanding manager.  Salary not bad for the work,
cons: Tired looking and tatty Contact Centre now we know why as  Lloyds Bank is closing the Contact Centre in June 2019.  Very pressurized with inbound calls every three seconds and up to 120 calls a day.  No room at all to progress in the bank.   The bank not transparent or truthful

advice: More staff recognition and provide opportunities to progress.
pros: Great place, autonomy and ability to drive own career goals with development and training. Plenty of opportunity to fix issues (if you like that type of stuff) and make a difference. A great balance of BAU work and project/change work.
cons: Extremely long hours, too many legacy systems which means issues of data quality. There is not the recognition culture as preached by Exec leadership lower down. Management does not appear to be interested in developing the future leaders as they are performance/ deliverables focused. ....... Shame, they will end up losing great talent to competitions.

summary: Not paid that well for finance..but easy work
advice: Hire in a more rigorous way to avoid having a workforce of incapable peope
pros: Good work/life balance, many opportunities to rise within LBG and lots of chance to move into different areas of the bank if you want
cons: Problems with allowing people to float from one area to another is that you could be working with people who don't have a clue and are incompetent. Main concern when working here was the inability of LBG to hire people who could do a good job. Hard to get things done in the office. Too much political correctness.

advice: Explain how they work out sickness and holidays as a company. Does taking 92hrs back for me bein sick since nov 2015 to oct 2016.
pros: How are they able to take 252hrs hol entitlment and change it to 160 for a year as l have been long term sick. Is this correct. 13 years employee good company.
cons: Not happy at losing 92hrs including 2 bank hols still to come when l will be back at work. I read they could only take bank hols back.but cant work out how l am left with 160hrs from 252hrs. Employee help please

summary: Better workplace when it was HBOS, increasingly demanding and frustratingly bureaucratic since Lloyds takeover
advice: Reduce the expectation on staff to complete questionnaires, mandatory training (usually pointless, overlong, with patronisingly obvious information) and read numerous weekly emails from various levels of management telling staff how great things are, when they know or think otherwise.
pros: Decent salary, bonuses, staff mortgage rate, flexible working
cons: Too much form filling, training and general admin, reducing time available to do actual work... or rather have to work additional unpaid hours to complete all work. Too many management layers (though it sems this is being addressed), poor communication leading to unclear responsibilities.

advice: If colleagues enjoy their work they are much more likely to provide an excellent service. Give us a bit more trust.
pros: Good basic pay, great pension, lots of company benefits such as sharesave, free private medical care, lots of flex options and brilliant holiday allowence.
cons: Micro-managed! No control over own diary, managers under the impression that mortgage admin does not exist therefore no time allowed to be blocked out to do this. Not interested in quality of work or enjoyment purely interested in how many life insurance quotes have been done even though there are no targets.

advice: Stop changing the goalposts constantly, cut out the red tape, and stop contradicting yourselves at every opportunity.
pros: Some of the projects you are assigned as an IPM are very interesting, especially some of the integration work.  Fairly broad choice of locations to work from, good if you like travel.  Flex benefits and staff discounts are handy if you have a mortgage or one of the AVA accounts with one of the Lloyds brands.
cons:
There is far too much change going on at once.  I had 5 managers in 18 months, resulting in very little chance to progress.  You are encouraged to apply for roles internally, although in all the time I was there I never once saw a higher grade IPM role appear on their jobshop site.  Salaries are fairly bad unless you negotiate a really good one at the start. Permanent staff in Service Delivery seem to get the raw end of the deal compared to other areas.   

Projects are supposed to be aligned to location, so for example I worked in Leeds, so I should get projects where the resources are in Leeds.  Quite frequently I was assigned to anything, meaning a lot of trips to Edinburgh, London, and occasionally Manchester.  There is a no travel week each month, but in general you're just expected to put in extra effort on the other 3 weeks where you can travel to the other sites.

There is a tendency to assume you know everything that has been discussed at the top (i.e. new policies) even though your day to day job means you never get given this information.  If you challenge this you are belittled and treated as if you should spend 23 hours a day dedicated to work.  The work life balance is shocking - if you're not regularly putting in over 45 hours a week, you're questioned why not.  If you're a contractor though, you're laughing all the way to the bank.  Expect to be extended repeatedly, earning a lot of money through the process.

Spending cuts are probably the most negative aspect.  Every last penny has to be justified through a bureaucratic system of red tape.  Just getting the job done is a tedious and long drawn out affair at the best of times.  There are a lot of very lazy people there, and also a lot of really good ones.  Most have no concept of project priorities leaving you in the firing line when dates slip through no fault of your own.
 
It's very much a place of not what you know but who you know.  You could be one of the most shocking employees in the world but if you're in with the senior management, you're untouchable.

summary: Good exposure to senior leaders and good work-life balance- scheme unchallenging at times.
advice: I personally feel that for such a large firm the management is very strong. With a clear vision and direction for the company which almost all colleagues have bought in to.
pros: Work-life balance is second to none. Management is usually very flexible and understanding, but you also feel like you are making a real difference to the progression of the group
cons: Work can lack challenge and there is a lot of moving around which some people may not like.

summary: I should have valued them more!
pros:
Very organised business
Good Managers and Senior Managers
They let you know what is expected of you
Company car due to amount of travel

I wish I never left and as they only advertise the entry level jobs I doubt I will find a job to apply for again at this company.
cons: So many moaners within the company and I got sucked in by it. Did not realise until I had left the company that it was actually a very positive place to be.

summary: Disappointing, lack of progression and office politics
advice: Support staffs progression needs fairly, offer incentives to stay and retain trained staff rather then recruit staff with no trade experience on the equivalent of a promotion. Who will be trained by the people who applied for the promotions with trade experience

Friendly staff
Push for trade qualifications
Relaxed atmosphere
Lots of push for staff to make sure they fit within the values and behaviours
cons:
Lack of progression
Monotonous process
Fragmented process
Promotion favouritism 
Promotions not issues on merit more being in the right place at the right time if your face fits

advice: treat your employees better you cant make honey if you kill all the bees.

cons:

cons: Too much paperwork and bureaucracy to get anything done.  Feels like paperwork with no purpose, although this could be a downfall for any large traditional bank.

summary: It's too big a bank to progress within

pros:
Money and benefits are good. 
A wide range of more junior staff are good at their jobs. Lots of training opportunities. If you wanted to , you could hide there until you retire!
cons: People are low priority, the IT sucks, HR is more do it yourself, good people management is rare. Little opportunity to travel.

summary: Working for Lloyds in the City
pros:
Good pay and benefits - private healthcare etc
Travelling with work - business class flights and nice hotels 
Some really enthusiastic managers with passion. 
Quite friendly and sociable 
Most people are pretty nice 
Flexible working and working from home days
Quite caring when I was hospitalised!
cons:
One of the offices in the City is a bit run down. 
Limited career opportunites if you are secretarial - you have to push to progress as you get pigeon holed working as a personal assistant. 
Training courses seemed to be limited.

summary: Clear vision from top management. People focussed

Always a role for those willing to be flexible

Varied Roles
Great Colleagues

Job roles and reporting structures are top heavy - no one to do the work but plenty to think up new work to do
Career development has all but gone

advice: Line managers desperately need training in how to manage their teams, and they need to learn how to see people as human beings rather than just numbers and statistics.
pros:
Great commitment to diversity and inclusion
Friendly and kind colleagues
Lots of money raised for charity, colleagues were always raising funds for a number of great causes.
cons:
Extremely poor computer infrastructure -- still using XP! 
Office wasn't kept clean -- there were mice found!
Line managers have no idea what they are doing most of the time
In the end I was sacked for taking too much time off sick, though I have multiple disabilities to deal with & was one of the best performers in my team.

summary: Great work life balance - at a cost

pros:
- Great work life/balance
- Big push for "Agile" working
- Genuinely friendly and relaxed people
- Big push to change culture
cons:
- Pay is reflective of the work/life balance, underpaid here vs the market significantly

- Lots of people here are cruising along and happy to do so - can be extremely frustrating

summary: A highly disorganised company and customers are usually treated unfairly.
advice: Please hire upper management that are not sociopaths. There is a good reason the public do not trust the banking industry.
pros: Nice building and facilities. One can meet great people here, due to the sheer size of hired staff.
cons:
Where does one start? Your experience highly depends on  which line manager is gifted to you. 

Processes and technology are cumbersome, outdated and produced by people who have little insight into the work that is being done by case handlers.

If you are employed as a contractor, it’s pretty much cut-throat in places but not in all areas.

advice: Put LBG’s values into action and be a good example of what aspiring leaders should seek to be, even if it goes against “the norm”.
pros: Great pay and benefits. There is also plenty of learning and development workshops. The exposure to senior leaders and opportunities to use the “grad card” are very insightful.
cons: Compulsory movement of placements (throughout the UK) in the graduate scheme can be expensive and a hassle. Short length of placements make it difficult to realistically get a better than average performance rating, particularly as a great deal of your time is dedicated to a professional qualification. There is also an inconsistent approach to the expectations of a graduate from line managers, cohort leads and others within LBG.

advice: Spend more time on the floor, people really aren't doing much work. Change is slow, bureaucracy is rife, often for no reason.
pros:
Grad scheme can be worthwhile if you get good placements, not guaranteed. 
Opportunity to work for one of the UKs biggest companies 
Very clear values set by Board of Directors that do trickle down throughout the company
CEO is very good.
cons:
Middle management can be full of egos
Financial penalties for those leaving the grad scheme regardless of reason
Professional Qualification (Chartered Banker) not recognized widely 
Tendency to have meetings for meetings sake, with no desired outcomes. Result is really "busy" people not making any tangible business improvements.
The leaving process needs to be improved, tax issues and reference issues experienced.

summary: good pay; personal development process slow; cliquey

Had a horrible personal experience with manager, who would constantly pick me up on 1/2 bad points in calls, and show no encouragement with 17/18 other good points. Personal and learning development is SLOW.

Good learning opportunities with plenty of responsibility and interesting work.
Full of genuinely nice people who are very good at the soft stuff (work-life balance etc).

cons:
Appear to pay less than other clearing banks for similar roles.
Unlikely to be a larger player than it currently is.
Anything IT related is useless.
Fair share of people who have worked for the bank for their whole career and are looking for a quite life to see out the last few years to retirement.

Working 8-7 effectively paid 9-4

advice:

All degree backgrounds welcomed - non-finance backgrounds not at a disadvantage

summary: Good for experience, but that's all

advice:
In the words of Richard Branson, 'Customers do not come first. Employees come first. If you take care of your employees, they will take care of the customers.'

As for my advice to customers, phone up and complain, you'll end the call with at least £50. (Unfortunately, it might take you an hour and half to get through, because like occurred in my training group, there will be a mass exodus of staff due to the appalling training and treatment they receive. This company will always be under-resourced and will continue to deliver the appalling level of customer service, Lloyd's Banking Group customers have become used to, if they don't change their policies and attitude very quickly).
pros: None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. None. (Hope this satisfy's the 20 word minimum).
cons:
This was the most horrendous experience of my entire professional career. The training was virtually non-existent. Eight weeks of training were scheduled, for six weeks I sat doing nothing because I had no systems. I took my first call on my last day of training and from there on in taught myself the job. With angry customers, who had usually queued for hours shouting at me down the phone (not exactly what I would call, the best bank for customers).

Furthermore, the 'flexible approach to life and work' the company boast about is again non-existent. It is virtually impossible to get any holidays approved. Shift slides are rare and when available fill up in minutes. Breaks are timed to the second. If you run over by 30 seconds, you will be questioned and asked to justify why you were late back. In this regard, it is genuinely worse than being back at primary school. 

The management are unhelpful, unapproachable and condescending. I had to approach managers I had never even been introduced to, to ask for help. On one occasion, after explaining another one of my many gaps in training, a manager responded to me by saying "what can you actually do." I can honestly say I have never been more insulted during my entire professional career. I am a law graduate, who was interested in pursuing a full time career within the company, but ultimately I have run a mile when I seen the behavior and negative attitude of managers and their treatment of staff. This is not an environment I would wish to work in ever again.  

On the whole, I felt extremely undervalued during my entire time at the company and found the whole experience traumatic, isolating, demeaning and unnecessarily stressful. I can honestly say that I will never work for this group again, I will never become a customer of this company and I will advise every person I ever into a banking discussion with, to stay well clear of all three brands (i.e Halifax, Bank of Scotland and Lloyds).

summary: Hopefully the business has changed somewhat in the last 4 years. It treated me VERY badly.
pros:
- It's a job. 
- Lots of mid management positions if that's what you like
cons:
The business expected lots of unpaid hours to be worked for any chance of promotion from the lower ranks and put an unfair amount of pressure on low paid workers whilst expecting them to have a smile on your face at all times, penalising you for saying anything negative about the company. Employees were commended for reporting other employees for speaking negatively too so there was a real backstabbing culture whilst I was there. Even a comment regarding the (now former) CEO's very public globetrotting love affairs would get you in trouble and gain brownie points for anonymous informants. Not a particularly pleasant or good place for your mental health or if you have a young family or other commitments outside of office hours! Also the technical infrastructure was atrocious, and the IT hardware was laughable. I hope the company have seriously invested in this side of the business, since I left with a big smile on my face, because I don't know how they would continue to retain staff or service their customers effectively otherwise. 

You were expected to write an essay each month for your ongoing performance review which was amazingly time consuming and stressful on top of a very heavy BAU workload where i would often not get any downtime in a day. Interviews were conducted on a point scoring process and points were given for corporate buzz words which really doesn't suit some peoples style; they would seriously overlook some talented and creative employees whilst taking on others would knew how to 'play the game'. On the other hand, some managers would manipulate the interview scores to employ people who they wanted in advance so there was no consistency in that respect. 

In all the companies I have worked for, pre and post Lloyds, I have never been anywhere that has been quite so big on brainwashing their staff into believing that where they are is the only the place to be, and I can tell you it certainly isn't. We were always told things like the salaries were no better elsewhere; false; the employee benefits were amazing; false, that the management were amazing; false, the grass is rarely ever greener on the other side; false.

I sincerely hope that the culture has changed dramatically and that the particular area that I spent a god few years of my life working in was a bad example of life at Lloyds. I would NEVER consider working there again.

summary: Lloyds used to be a great place to work

advice: Streamline processes, and take some of the admin work off the RMs where possible

advice: Possibly introduce rotations to give interns a variation of the different areas within the credit risk arm. This would provide a whole understanding of this area rather than one specific area.

summary: Dreadful in every sense of the word
advice: Get rid of half the TM’s and SME’s that take power-trips. Abandon giving out pointless ‘Rocs’ to people who are trying their best. Make customers self-serve a bit more and empower staff to not tolerate abusive behaviour. Get rid of your bureaucracy and putting top management first.
pros: Staff mortgage and that is all
cons: Dreadful hours, most of the managers in Belfast Gasworks are awful with the exception of the odd few. You’re constantly expected to give 300% and get little in return. Morale is low, time off is non-existent and the customer is right even when cursing and swearing at you. My final straw was a manager who became extremely aggressive with me after I took some nasty abuse from a customer, before I walked out on the sick and got a job with a decent financial institution. Staff leave in droves and it’s no wonder. Time off the phone is constantly pulled for ‘amber alerts’ which is the biggest pile of nonsense. Branch calls get routed through to call centre because too lazy or too understaffed and customer’s hate this. Not enough is done to encourage customers to self-serve for silly things like balances and savings renewals. If you disagree with a manager or ‘what the business thinks’ you’re classed as having a behavioural problem. Take a day off sick?? - they practically want to know your every trip to the toilet and how many times you’ve blown your nose when you complete your return to work - plus they won’t give you peace to rest and recover. Awful awful place!! Tactical planning and scheduling - don’t get me started on that front - horrific to get a shift change even in an emergency and if in the rare event it is granted you are reminded of ‘that time the business did you a favour’. If you are thinking about working here - do not bother. The most bureaucratic and inefficient company with systems and processes that are not suitable in this day and age. They claim to ‘put customers first, keep it simple and make a difference together’. Let’s be 100% clear - the business comes first - NOT the customer and the processes make this abundantly clear. The business needs come second, then the customer comes somewhere down the pecking order. Staff are not important in any shape, form or fashion.

advice: Adapt a common sense approach.  Job title should be team leader and not team manager, as unable to manage much. Forget hierarchy attitude. Terrible location, not convenient to local amenities, shop a the gasworks closed on weekends, canteen in building closed on Sundays and early every other day. Would not recommend anyone to work here.

pros: The salary did increase over time but this was a blanket increase and other staff who were under-performing also got pay rises.
cons:
Although I used to work a Lloyds I am not a 'bitter' ex-employee, what I have to say comes from a place of concern, for staff and the vulnerable customers which are supported within in Hove - Customer Priority Team. 
Firstly there was a lack of proper training, the management felt that sticking you in a room for days was a good use of resourcing when it would take 30 minutes to run through the information in a morning meeting (leaving other colleagues on the phone struggling). There was no trust in employees, even if you were the perfect person, taking less than your allocated breaks and scoring perfectly on reviews they would still be checking your every move and question you constantly. When I joined the team supporting our most vulnerable customers they only positioned the role as 'Are you a good listener, we can teach you everything else', so a severe lack of transparency. From when I joined to when I left which was 11 months, I passed all of my calls. In the first three months I passed all my calls and was propping up the rest of the new intake. The management then said as part of passing the first stage everyone needs to pass3 months of calls, which I had already completed but they stated that didn't count. Then after being in the role for 6 months a new manager, which was flown in on the graduate scheme said I was doing so well that in another 9 months they might consider me for the talent program. Any progression was very slow and they seemed to want to keep me on the phones just to boost their own figures. 
There is no internal support structure for staff. Some of the calls were dealing with people with terminal cancer or suicide, ranging to people self-harming, severe poverty and depression. They stopped staff from sitting near close colleagues, so there was no one to offload after 2-3 hour long calls. You were expected to get right back on the phone and quickly move on. After a very traumatic call I was given the details of the free counselling service. I called and spoke with a qualified counsellor who was horrified and advised that she was taking pretty much the same types of calls but was getting paid significantly more, had to have a debrief with her line manager ever few days and could always sit down with a colleague after any difficult calls. I mentioned that my colleagues would go home and cry due to the distressing nature of the calls and several had left due to depression.  She said that they counselling service could come in to support staff but when I suggested this, it was turned down. 
The main reason why I left was that there was no career progression whatsoever even for someone meeting all targets, who trained others, got involved in charity events and was team leader on monthly initiatives such as myself. 
Another reason was the severe lack of empathy and care for Lloyds customers. People would be heavily swearing on the floor, laughing while people were taking very distressing calls or were left without any management on whilst they had meetings, so there was sometimes no point of escalation or support and you had to rely on the support of other colleagues.
They also changed their policy, which is now widely known and raised charges on their overdrafts to force people to take out loans with them to then remove the overdraft. This might seem like a good idea to some of you but this then forces the vulnerable person to then pay interest at higher levels and if they cannot pay they reduced the time to 3 months and then the individual has around 60 days before they get a 6 year default (black mark) against their credit file. This effects peoples financial history for a long time and management were all too quick to not tailor solutions to the customer and start them on the path to a default. 
Temporary members of staff and permanent employees are treated differently and do not received the same benefits even though they worked just as hard. 
The hours were excessive and you were expected to stay on after your shift had finished, they won't pay overtime but will give you the time back but only ever at the start of your shift - highly inflexible. I once had 4 hours of time owed from one week so they had to give me a half-day - not ideal for work-life balance at all.

summary: Not recommending to take a job
advice:
You really need to change the leadership team from Directors - down to and including Senior managers. Bring new people on board, coming from outside Lloyds if you'd like to survive on market that is now opening to FINTECH companies and services.
You need an accelerated process of management and processes review and restructure. The bank is still on the market due to inertia, but professional people won't accept to work back in a '70-'80 type of organization.
pros: nice technical staff, work life balance
cons:
Low quality management, starting from Senior management up to CIO. A culture of 'please your manager' is pushed from top to down and aggressively protected. Promotion based on who you know and please not based on what you know, what yo prove you can do, what value you've added and can add.
Change and continuous improvement - is mentioned in papers as it sounds good, but in practice, if you just try to suggest a change of the current way of working you'll be strongly shut down with 'This is how Lloyds do it'.. 
Challenge and empowerment - not accepted and if you have the nerve to challenge your manager, you'll have to expect bad evaluation regardless your excellent feedback from all stakeholders. It is simply forbidden to have different opinion that your manager or any other manager and to express that, trying to show them a different view, an alternative or simply to clarify what they want.
Ideas and 'innovation' are only accepted if coming from top to down. It is not in management agenda to listen to ideas coming from down to top.. 
Rapid process of de-professionalization if working in this environment. Project planning and project assignment is something unknown for most of the employees. Importance of planning, why is required, what is used for etc have been organized as a 'mandatory' course by the end of last year for all employees of that part of Lloyds business.. 
Roles and responsibilities unclear -  the senior manager doesn't understand the importance of roles and responsibilities. He's view of managing a team is that the team does what he says when he says..and this is the situation in all other teams in the same area of business. 
Too many employees with more than 15 years in Lloyds. I don't know what is the average / LBG, but in department I've been working for, that was on a rate of 95%. 
This is holding the bank to change, to adopt new ideas, to innovate, to give up on current way of evaluation that is totally subjective and in hands of direct line manager.

summary: Lloyds to not, up to you!
advice:
Go back to reviewing people on how they have performed over the year.  
It's most likely way to late as too many have already been made redundant but undo the damage done to your IT teams, also get the support of your business critical applications\systems back on shore before an RBS happens.
pros: Good package and bonus can be good for some.
cons:
Review process - Behavioral Scoring as they call it and the bell curve which means that within any team there should always be a percentage that exceed, meet and, fail to deliver as expected.  For the lucky few this can be very rewarding but not for the majority as your not so much rated on your own performance but that of any other colleague, that's anyone in a similar roll to you anywhere in the organization, as if you are in a team were you are head and shoulders above the rest nice bonus for you, but not so if you are in a team of equally talented individuals.  It's way to easy for management to justify whatever mark they have decided to give you, helps if your face fits or your good friends with your line manager!  It is supposed to spur you on to be as good as the individual your were marked against but if you have bust you ass for the last 6 months, gone out your way, above and beyond whatever ... things the used to give you a good rating, it can be very de-motivating.  

Off sharing - If you are a developer who doesn't want to spend his days reviewing work delivered from off shore (a lot of poor quality work it has to be said), then Lloyds isn't the place for you, their IT policy  at the moment is off shore all development and support, hard to stay on top of your development skills when your not going to be doing any development!

summary: Poor Pay Practices and Shocking Place to Work for
advice: Stop concentrating on penalising your workers, focus on the larger sums of cash further up the chain at C level as you're going to alienate yourselves.

cons:
Bullies are fester despite causing unrest and issues for others.
The CEO is paid millions and has affairs whilst the share price tanks, however an honest hard worker who leaves within 6 months of receiving a bonus will have to repay the amount. If this is unknown at the time, Lloyds will not hesitate in calling the bailiffs on you and pressing CCJs - read the small print and trying their best to dismantle your career.
There is a lot of marketing material on mental health, very little is put into practice.
They embrace digital, yet I have witnessed meetings in which graduates who want to talk about technologies are shut down by senior management.
Lloyds hired thousands of contractors on a ring fencing programme that was failing due to mis management - it would be good to know the cost of their programme against other leading banks.
Management from the old HBOS which failed were brought in to run their entire operations! I'd even question their commercial and business sense. 
Some of the internal processes are very manual and the only means of improving them or adding value from an ops perspective is to race to the bottom and make graduates do the boring work, as the management will not invest time and effort to coach them, mentor them and develop them to improve those processes.
When things go wrong, it turns into a blame game.
Very few opportunities for progression. Most people work in the same role or move laterally like a merry go round for at least 10 years. 
You will be expected to work into late hours, for no additional pay and only to compensate for poor practices.

advice: Stop putting so much pressure on colleagues to sell products, that’s not what we are there for.  Understand that when employees are calling in sick it’s because of the huge amounts of pressure.  Change attitude towards sales and back to relationship management.

Wages are terrible, I’ve worked there for 4 years and still happen to be under the UK average wage despite having a degree. The sales environment is back and there is huge amounts of pressure to sell products to customers, and they are even teaching people how to “overcome objections” from customers who refuse to take a product. All the bank looks at is numbers and how many products you are selling. Interviews are now recorded and managers will go back through recordings to create ammunition for a case to give you a disciplinary or to create an “action plan” which soon leads to disciplinaries. If you’re not selling enough products they want you out, despite them claiming that it’s “all about relationships”. It’s very hard to get a promotion, very authoritative and clique-y. They will not pay any overtime despite you getting in half hour early and finishing half hour late every single day. Bonuses are terrible. Would not recommend for a long term career, just a stepping stone. The stress is not worth the money at all. They treat a 25k job like a 70k+ job with responsibilities and pressure they create.

- Leaders don't demonstrate the integrity or the expertise you would expect from executives.
